Exact finite-core clearance\n\nFor any point \\(X\\), the nearest distance to the persistent ring worldsheet is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD(X,\\Sigma)=\n\\sqrt{(r-a)^2+z^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor \\(T_{p,q}\\),\n\n\\[\nr-a=\\rho\\cos qt,\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nz=\\rho\\sin qt.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\nD^2\n&=\n\\rho^2\\cos^2 qt+\n\\rho^2\\sin^2 qt\\\\\n&=\\rho^2.\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nHence,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD(T_{p,q},\\Sigma)=\\rho.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is independent of both \\(p\\) and \\(q\\).\n\nFor the numerical fixture,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD=0.5.\n}\n\\]\n\nChoose a combined finite-core exclusion thickness\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\delta+\\epsilon=0.2.\n}\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD=0.5>0.2.\n}\n\\]\n\nEvery tested toroidal probe remains separated from the ring support.\n\nThe independent winding values do not arise from a collision or singular configuration.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Exact squared-gradient diagnostic\n\nDifferentiate the toroidal curve.\n\nWrite\n\n\\[\nr(t)=a+\\rho\\cos qt.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\nr'(t)=-\\rho q\\sin qt.\n\\]\n\nThe spatial velocity components satisfy\n\n\\[\n\\dot x^2+\\dot y^2\n=\n(r')^2+p^2r^2.\n\\]\n\nThe vertical derivative is\n\n\\[\n\\dot z=\\rho q\\cos qt.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\|\\dot T_{p,q}\\|^2\n&=\n\\rho^2q^2\\sin^2 qt\\\\\n&\\quad+\np^2(a+\\rho\\cos qt)^2\\\\\n&\\quad+\n\\rho^2q^2\\cos^2 qt.\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nUsing\n\n\\[\n\\sin^2 qt+\\cos^2 qt=1,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\|\\dot T_{p,q}\\|^2\n=\n\\rho^2q^2+\np^2(a+\\rho\\cos qt)^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nDefine the geometric squared-gradient diagnostic\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG_{p,q}=\n\\int_0^{2\\pi}\n\\|\\dot T_{p,q}\\|^2dt.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor nonzero integer \\(q\\),\n\n\\[\n\\int_0^{2\\pi}\\cos qt\\,dt=0\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\int_0^{2\\pi}\\cos^2qt\\,dt=\\pi.\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG_{p,q}\n=\n2\\pi\n\\left[\n\\rho^2q^2+\np^2\\left(a^2+\\frac{\\rho^2}{2}\\right)\n\\right],\n\\qquad q\\neq0.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor \\(q=0\\),\n\n\\[\nr=a+\\rho\n\\]\n\nis constant, giving\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG_{p,0}=2\\pi p^2(a+\\rho)^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nThese are exact geometrical expressions, not physical energy laws.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Numerical results\n\nThe executed calculation used\n\n\\[\na=2,\\qquad \\rho=0.5.\n\\]\n\n| \\((p,q)\\) | Orbital \\(B\\) | Meridional \\(n\\) | Minimum separation | Exact \\(G\\) |\n|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n| (1,0) | 1 | 0 | 0.5 | 39.269908170 |\n| (0,1) | 0 | 1 | 0.5 | 1.570796327 |\n| (1,1) | 1 | 1 | 0.5 | 27.488935719 |\n| (2,3) | 2 | 3 | 0.5 | 117.809724510 |\n| (3,2) | 3 | 2 | 0.5 | 239.546439836 |\n| (0,3) | 0 | 3 | 0.5 | 14.137166941 |\n| (4,0) | 4 | 0 | 0.5 | 628.318530718 |\n\nIndependent numerical quadrature agreed with the exact squared-gradient expressions to within\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n1.5\\times10^{-14}.\n}\n\\]\n\nSampled phase unwrapping reproduced every integer winding.\n\nThe important comparison is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n(1,0)\\quad\\text{versus}\\quad(0,1).\n}\n\\]\n\nBoth are disjoint from the ring support.\n\nOne has orbital winding without meridional linking.\n\nThe other has meridional linking without orbital winding.\n\nTherefore, the ring-meridional invariant cannot simply be identified with BR-006's cumulative orbital braid count.\n\n---\n\n# 8. Explicit contraction of an orbital longitude\n\nThe independence result can be sharpened.\n\nTake the orbital longitude\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nC_0(t)=\n(2.5\\cos t,2.5\\sin t,0,0).\n}\n\\]\n\nThis loop makes one complete azimuthal revolution around the central axis.\n\nIts meridional winding is zero.\n\nI constructed the following continuous deformation:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nC_s(t)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n2.5(1-s)\\cos t\\\\\n2.5(1-s)\\sin t\\\\\n2\\sin(\\pi s)\\\\\n0\n\\end{pmatrix},\n\\qquad0\\leq s\\leq1.\n}\n\\]\n\nAt\n\n\\[\ns=0,\n\\]\n\nwe recover the original orbital longitude.\n\nAt\n\n\\[\ns=1,\n\\]\n\nthe curve becomes\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nC_1(t)=(0,0,0,0).\n}\n\\]\n\nIt has contracted to a point.\n\nThe deformation moves the loop upward out of the ring plane, reduces its radius, and then returns to the origin.\n\nThe ring worldsheet is never intersected.\n\n### Exact clearance function\n\nThe loop radius is\n\n\\[\nr_s=2.5(1-s).\n\\]\n\nIts vertical coordinate is\n\n\\[\nz_s=2\\sin(\\pi s).\n\\]\n\nTherefore, the distance to the ring worldsheet is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD(s)=\n\\sqrt{\n[2.5(1-s)-2]^2+\n4\\sin^2(\\pi s)\n}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis function is independent of the loop parameter \\(t\\).\n\nA numerical minimization gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_{\\min}=0.464497372422\n}\n\\]\n\nat\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ns=0.027452651259.\n}\n\\]\n\nSince\n\n\\[\n0.464497372422>0.2,\n\\]\n\nthe deformation preserves finite-core separation.\n\n---\n\n# 9. Rigorous clearance bound\n\nThe numerical minimum is useful, but a proof does not require trusting the optimizer.\n\nPartition the deformation interval into three regions.\n\n### Region I\n\nFor\n\n\\[\n0\\leq s\\leq0.1,\n\\]\n\nthe radial offset satisfies\n\n\\[\nr_s-a\n=\n2.5(1-s)-2\n\\geq0.25.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD(s)\\geq0.25.\n}\n\\]\n\n### Region II\n\nFor\n\n\\[\n0.1\\leq s\\leq0.9,\n\\]\n\nthe vertical displacement satisfies\n\n\\[\nz_s=2\\sin(\\pi s)\n\\geq2\\sin(\\pi/10).\n\\]\n\nNumerically,\n\n\\[\n2\\sin(\\pi/10)=0.618033988750.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD(s)\\geq0.618033988750.\n}\n\\]\n\n### Region III\n\nFor\n\n\\[\n0.9\\leq s\\leq1,\n\\]\n\nthe radius satisfies\n\n\\[\nr_s\\leq0.25.\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n|r_s-a|\\geq1.75.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD(s)\\geq1.75.\n}\n\\]\n\nCombining the three intervals,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD(s)\\geq0.25\n}\n\\]\n\nthroughout the entire deformation.\n\nSince\n\n\\[\n0.25>0.2,\n\\]\n\nthe finite-core exclusion condition is satisfied rigorously.\n\nHence,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{The orbital longitude contracts without crossing the ring support.}\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is the decisive result of the turn.\n\n---\n\n# 10. Why the azimuthal winding can disappear\n\nInitially,\n\n\\[\n\\phi(t)=t.\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\nB=1.\n\\]\n\nThroughout the contraction for \\(s<1\\), the loop remains at positive radius and its azimuthal winding remains one.\n\nAt\n\n\\[\ns=1,\n\\]\n\nthe loop reaches the spatial axis\n\n\\[\nr=0.\n\\]\n\nThere, the azimuthal angle becomes undefined.\n\nBut this axis is not the ring worldsheet.\n\nThe ring support remains at\n\n\\[\nr=a=2,\\qquad z=0.\n\\]\n\nTherefore, the azimuthal winding can disappear through an admissible contraction that never crosses the protected codimension-two support.\n\nMeanwhile, the ring-meridional winding remains\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nn=0\n}\n\\]\n\nthroughout.\n\nThe distinction is therefore structural:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{Azimuthal winding is protected only if the axis or an equivalent constraint is excluded.}\n}\n\\]\n\nThe Kerr-ring worldsheet excludes its own meridional core, not automatically the central spatial axis.\n\n---\n\n# 11. Physical-worldline boundary\n\nThe toroidal curves above are closed spatial probes at fixed \\(w\\).\n\nThey are not particle worldlines in the H(s)H block universe.\n\nTo construct a monotone-\\(w\\) counterpart, set\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nw(t)=\\frac{L}{2\\pi}t.\n}\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\widetilde T_{p,q}(t)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n(a+\\rho\\cos qt)\\cos pt\\\\\n(a+\\rho\\cos qt)\\sin pt\\\\\n\\rho\\sin qt\\\\\nLt/(2\\pi)\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor integer \\(p,q\\), the spatial endpoint configuration repeats after \\(t=2\\pi\\).\n\nBut the fourth coordinate changes by\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta w=L.\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore, the curve is not closed in four-dimensional space.\n\nIts unwrapped angular changes remain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta\\phi=2\\pi p\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta\\theta=2\\pi q.\n}\n\\]\n\nThese quantities record distinct aspects of the history.\n\nHowever, neither is automatically a closed-loop topological invariant of the four-dimensional particle trajectory.\n\nBR-006's cumulative orbital braid is a history-dependent mechanical constraint by framework premise.\n\nThe ring-meridional integer is a complement-topology invariant of closed probes.\n\nAn actual derivation must connect those two structures through the admissible geometry of interacting worldtubes.\n\n---\n\n# 12. radius\n\n\\[\n\\epsilon=0.2,\n\\]\n\ntheir minimum clearance is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_{\\rm clearance}\n=\na-2\\epsilon\n=\n1.6.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe two complete four-dimensional finite-core worldtubes remain strictly disjoint throughout the entire deformation.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Where the orbital winding disappears\n\nThe projected orbital winding is defined using the transverse relative vector\n\n\\[\n\\mathbf r_\\perp=\n(n_x,n_y).\n\\]\n\nIts winding number is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nB=\n\\frac1{2\\pi}\n\\int_0^{2\\pi}\n\\frac{\nn_x\\,dn_y-n_y\\,dn_x\n}{\nn_x^2+n_y^2\n}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis expression is defined whenever\n\n\\[\nn_x^2+n_y^2>0.\n\\]\n\nFor\n\n\\[\ns<\\frac12,\n\\]\n\nthe complex circle\n\n\\[\n\\zeta_s(t)=s+(1-s)e^{it}\n\\]\n\nencloses the origin.\n\nThe transverse winding is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{B=1.}\n\\]\n\nFor\n\n\\[\ns>\\frac12,\n\\]\n\nthe circle no longer encloses the origin.\n\nThe transverse winding is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{B=0.}\n\\]\n\nAt the transition,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ns=\\frac12,\\qquad t=\\pi,\n}\n\\]\n\nwe have\n\n\\[\n\\zeta=0.\n\\]\n\nThe inverse stereographic map gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathbf n=(0,0,1).\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nn_x=n_y=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe transverse winding becomes undefined at this intermediate configuration.\n\nBut the actual spatial relative separation remains\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\|\\mathbf r\\|=a=2.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe worldtubes do not touch.\n\nThe orbital winding has disappeared by passing through a transverse-coordinate singularity, not through a physical centerline collision.\n\nThis is the exact mechanism that an additional physical interbraid constraint would have to forbid or otherwise account for.\n\n---\n\n# 8. Exact squared-gradient diagnostic\n\nDefine the spatial squared-gradient functional for one worldline:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG(s)=\n\\int_0^{2\\pi}\n\\left\\|\n\\frac{d}{dt}\n\\left(\n\\frac a2\\mathbf n_s(t)\n\\right)\n\\right\\|^2dt.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is a geometric diagnostic, not a physical energy law.\n\nUsing the stereographic metric,\n\n\\[\n\\left\\|\n\\frac{d}{dt}\n\\left(\n\\frac a2\\mathbf n_s\n\\right)\n\\right\\|^2\n=\n\\frac{a^2(1-s)^2}\n{\\left[A+B\\cos t\\right]^2},\n\\]\n\nwhere\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nA=1+s^2+(1-s)^2\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nB=2s(1-s).\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG(s)=\na^2(1-s)^2\n\\int_0^{2\\pi}\n\\frac{dt}{(A+B\\cos t)^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe exact integral is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\int_0^{2\\pi}\n\\frac{dt}{(A+B\\cos t)^2}\n=\n\\frac{2\\pi A}{(A^2-B^2)^{3/2}}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG(s)=\n\\frac{\n2\\pi a^2(1-s)^2 A\n}{\n(A^2-B^2)^{3/2}\n}.\n}\n\\]\n\nAt\n\n\\[\ns=0,\n\\]\n\nthe result is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG(0)=2\\pi\n\\approx6.283185307.\n}\n\\]\n\nAt the winding transition,\n\n\\[\ns=\\frac12,\n\\]\n\nthe result is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG(1/2)\n=\n\\frac{3\\pi}{2\\sqrt2}\n\\approx3.332162204.\n}\n\\]\n\nAt\n\n\\[\ns=1,\n\\]\n\nthe result is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG(1)=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe geometric gradient remains finite throughout the winding transition.\n\nNo infinite geometrical penalty arises from this minimal smooth-centerline construction.\n\nA physically derived constitutive rule could impose additional restrictions, but no such rule is assumed here.\n\n---\n\n# 9. θ₄ compatibility check\n\nUsing the fourth-coordinate direction as the time normal, the tangent angle is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\theta_4=\n\\arctan\n\\left(\n\\frac{\n(a/2)\\|\\partial_t\\mathbf n_s\\|\n}{\n\\kappa\n}\n\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe maximum possible angle in the tested deformation is bounded by\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\theta_{4,\\max}\n\\leq\n\\arctan\n\\left(\n\\frac{aL_{\\max}}{2\\kappa}\n\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nFor the selected Conditional protection by bounded transverse displacement\n\nNow impose a candidate geometrical restriction.\n\nLet the relative spatial displacement be\n\n\\[\n\\mathbf r_{\\rm rel}\n=\n(x_{\\rm rel},y_{\\rm rel},z_{\\rm rel}).\n\\]\n\nAssume its magnitude satisfies\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\|\\mathbf r_{\\rm rel}\\|\\geq a.\n}\n\\]\n\nAlso assume that its displacement perpendicular to the orbital plane is bounded:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|z_{\\rm rel}|\\leq H.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe transverse separation is\n\n\\[\n\\rho_\\perp^2\n=\nx_{\\rm rel}^2+y_{\\rm rel}^2.\n\\]\n\nSince\n\n\\[\n\\|\\mathbf r_{\\rm rel}\\|^2\n=\n\\rho_\\perp^2+z_{\\rm rel}^2,\n\\]\n\nwe have\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\rho_\\perp^2\n&=\n\\|\\mathbf r_{\\rm rel}\\|^2-z_{\\rm rel}^2\\\\\n&\\geq\na^2-H^2.\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\rho_\\perp\\geq\\sqrt{a^2-H^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nIf\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nH<a,\n}\n\\]\n\nthen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\rho_\\perp>0.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe transverse relative vector cannot pass through zero.\n\nHence its winding\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nB=\n\\frac1{2\\pi}\n\\int d\\arg(x_{\\rm rel}+iy_{\\rm rel})\n}\n\\]\n\nis invariant under continuous fixed-endpoint deformations satisfying that restriction.\n\nThis is a standard homotopy consequence, not a physical law imported into H(s)H.\n\n### Numerical clearance\n\nFor\n\n\\[\na=2,\n\\]\n\nthe executed calculation gives:\n\n| Maximum \\(\\lvert z_{\\rm rel}\\rvert\\) | Protected? | Minimum transverse separation |\n|---:|---|---:|\n| 0.00 | Yes | 2.000000000000 |\n| 0.50 | Yes | 1.936491673104 |\n| 1.00 | Yes | 1.732050807569 |\n| 1.80 | Yes | 0.871779788708 |\n| 1.99 | Yes | 0.199749843554 |\n| 2.00 | Not guaranteed | 0 |\n| 2.10 | Not guaranteed | 0 |\n\nThe mathematical boundary is exact:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nH=a.\n}\n\\]\n\nAt this boundary, the transverse separation can vanish while the full spatial separation remains nonzero.\n\n**H(s)H implication:** A genuine inherited restriction that prevents the relative displacement from reaching this boundary would protect orbital winding.\n\nBut such a restriction has not been derived merely by declaring that the tubes are finite-core objects.\n\n---\n\n# 6. A time-normal angle criterion\n\nA related condition can be expressed using a bound on worldtube inclination.\n\nSuppose the vertical spatial slopes of the two worldlines obey\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\left|\\frac{dz_\\pm}{dw}\\right|\n\\leq\n\\tan\\theta_{\\max}.\n}\n\\]\n\nHere the angle is measured from the fourth-coordinate direction, consistent with BR-005's time-normal convention.\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\left|\n\\frac{dz_{\\rm rel}}{dw}\n\\right|\n\\leq\n2\\tan\\theta_{\\max}.\n\\]\n\nAssume the relative vertical displacement vanishes at both endpoints:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nz_{\\rm rel}(0)=z_{\\rm rel}(W)=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor any intermediate point \\(w\\),\n\n\\[\n|z_{\\rm rel}(w)|\n\\leq\n2\\tan\\theta_{\\max}\n\\min(w,W-w).\n\\]\n\nSince\n\n\\[\n\\min(w,W-w)\\leq\\frac W2,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|z_{\\rm rel}(w)|\n\\leq\nW\\tan\\theta_{\\max}.\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore, a sufficient no-escape condition is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nW\\tan\\theta_{\\max}<a.\n}\n\\]\n\nEquivalently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\theta_{\\max}<\n\\arctan\\left(\\frac aW\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nFor the tested values:\n\n| \\(W\\) | Maximum sufficient angle |\n|---:|---:|\n| \\(4\\pi\\) | \\(9.043061079038^\\circ\\) |\n| 20 | \\(5.710593137500^\\circ\\) |\n| 40 | \\(2.862405226112^\\circ\\) |\n\nThis is a finite-history protection criterion.\n\nIt has a significant limitation.\n\nAs\n\n\\[\nW\\rightarrow\\infty,\n\\]\n\nthe sufficient angle bound approaches zero:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\arctan(a/W)\\rightarrow0.\n}\n\\]\n\nThus a fixed positive inclination limit cannot, by this argument alone, protect orbital winding over arbitrarily long histories.\n\nAn indefinitely persistent interbraid constraint requires more than this simple slope bound.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Minimum geometrical cost of an escape\n\nSuppose a winding change occurs at an intermediate fourth-coordinate value\n\n\\[\nw_0\\in(0,W).\n\\]\n\nAt the transition,\n\n\\[\n\\rho_\\perp(w_0)=0.\n\\]\n\nIf the full relative spatial separation is at least \\(a\\), then\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|z_{\\rm rel}(w_0)|\\geq a.\n}\n\\]\n\nAssume again that\n\n\\[\nz_{\\rm rel}(0)=z_{\\rm rel}(W)=0.\n\\]\n\nBy the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality,\n\n\\[\n\\left|\n\\int_0^{w_0}z_{\\rm rel}'(w)\\,dw\n\\right|^2\n\\leq\nw_0\n\\int_0^{w_0}[z_{\\rm rel}'(w)]^2dw.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\int_0^{w_0}[z_{\\rm rel}']^2dw\n\\geq\n\\frac{a^2}{w_0}.\n}\n\\]\n\nApplying the same argument between \\(w_0\\) and \\(W\\),\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\int_{w_0}^{W}[z_{\\rm rel}']^2dw\n\\geq\n\\frac{a^2}{W-w_0}.\n}\n\\]\n\nAdding,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\int_0^W[z_{\\rm rel}']^2dw\n\\geq\na^2\n\\left(\n\\frac1{w_0}+\\frac1{W-w_0}\n\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe right-hand side is minimized at\n\n\\[\nw_0=\\frac W2.\n\\]\n\nHence,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\int_0^W[z_{\\rm rel}']^2dw\n\\geq\n\\frac{4a^2}{W}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor symmetric worldlines,\n\n\\[\nz_\\pm=\\pm\\frac{z_{\\rm rel}}2,\n\\]\n\nthe combined vertical squared-gradient is\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\nE_z\n&=\n\\int_0^W\n\\left[\n(z_+')^2+(z_-')^2\n\\right]dw\\\\\n&=\n\\frac12\n\\int_0^W(z_{\\rm rel}')^2dw.\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE_z\\geq\\frac{2a^2}{W}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is a rigorous lower bound for a geometrical diagnostic.\n\nIt is not an independently established physical energy.\n\nThe scaling is the important feature:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE_{z,\\min}\\propto W^{-1}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe minimum required squared-gradient becomes smaller as the available fourth-coordinate extent grows.\n\n---\n\n# 8. Smooth finite-cost excursion\n\nThe preceding bound can be compared with an explicit smooth excursion.\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\nu(w)=\n\\frac{2\\min(w,W-w)}{W}.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n0\\leq u\\leq1.\n\\]\n\nUse the cubic smoothstep function\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nf(u)=3u^2-2u^3.\n}\n\\]\n\nConstruct\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nz_{\\rm rel}(w)=af(u(w)).\n}\n\\]\n\nThis satisfies\n\n\\[\nz_{\\rm rel}(0)=0,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nz_{\\rm rel}(W/2)=a,\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nz_{\\rm rel}(W)=0.\n\\]\n\nIts first derivative vanishes at the endpoints and at the midpoint.\n\nThe required integrals are\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\int_0^1[f'(u)]^2du=\\frac65\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\int_0^1[f''(u)]^2du=12.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe combined vertical squared-gradient for symmetric tubes is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE_z^{\\rm smooth}\n=\n\\frac{12a^2}{5W}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe combined vertical squared-curvature is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK_z^{\\rm smooth}\n=\n\\frac{96a^2}{W^3}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThese are finite.\n\nFor\n\n\\[\na=2,\\qquad W=4\\pi,\n\\]\n\nthe values are\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE_z^{\\rm smooth}=0.763943726841\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK_z^{\\rm smooth}=0.193509206599.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor\n\n\\[\nW=40,\n\\]\n\nthey become\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE_z^{\\rm smooth}=0.240000000000\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK_z^{\\rm smooth}=0.006000000000.\n}\n\\]\n\nIndependent numerical quadrature reproduced both curvature values.\n\nThis excursion is a vertical-displacement comparison, not by itself a complete orbital-unwinding homotopy. The Aldus family supplies the complete homotopy.\n\n---\n\n# 9. Exact gradient of the complete unwinding homotopy\n\nFor one worldline, define\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG(s)=\n\\int_0^{2\\pi}\n\\left\\|\n\\frac{d}{dt}\n\\left(\n\\frac a2\\mathbf n_s(t)\n\\right)\n\\right\\|^2dt.\n}\n\\]\n\nLet\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nA=1+s^2+(1-s)^2\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nB=2s(1-s).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe inverse stereographic metric gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\left\\|\n\\frac{d}{dt}\n\\left(\n\\frac a2\\mathbf n_s\n\\right)\n\\right\\|^2\n=\n\\frac{a^2(1-s)^2}\n{(A+B\\cos t)^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\nG(s)=\na^2(1-s)^2\n\\int_0^{2\\pi}\n\\frac{dt}{(A+B\\cos t)^2}.\n\\]\n\nUsing\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\int_0^{2\\pi}\n\\frac{dt}{(A+B\\cos t)^2}\n=\n\\frac{2\\pi A}{(A^2-B^2)^{3/2}},\n}\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG(s)=\n\\frac{\n2\\pi a^2(1-s)^2A\n}{\n(A^2-B^2)^{3/2}\n}.\n}\n\\]\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE=s^2-s+1\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nC=2s^2-2s+1.\n}\n\\]\n\nSince\n\n\\[\nA=2E\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nA^2-B^2=4C,\n\\]\n\nthe expression simplifies to\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG(s)=\n\\frac{\\pi a^2}{2}\n\\frac{\n(1-s)^2E\n}{\nC^{3/2}\n}.\n}\n\\]\n\nExplicitly,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG(s)=\n\\frac{\\pi a^2}{2}\n\\frac{\n(1-s)^2(s^2-s+1)\n}{\n(2s^2-2s+1)^{3/2}\n}.\n}\n\\]\n\n---\n\n# 10. Proof that the gradient strictly decreases\n\nDifferentiate the logarithm:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{d}{ds}\\log G(s)\n=\n\\frac{\ns(2s^3-3s^2+2s+1)\n}{\n(s-1)(s^2-s+1)(2s^2-2s+1)\n}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor\n\n\\[\n0<s<1,\n\\]\n\nthe factor\n\n\\[\ns>0.\n\\]\n\nAlso,\n\n\\[\n2s^3-3s^2+2s+1\n=\n1+s(2s^2-3s+2).\n\\]\n\nThe quadratic\n\n\\[\n2s^2-3s+2\n\\]\n\nhas discriminant\n\n\\[\n\\Delta=9-16=-7.\n\\]\n\nIts leading coefficient is positive, so\n\n\\[\n2s^2-3s+2>0.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n2s^3-3s^2+2s+1>0.\n}\n\\]\n\nMeanwhile,\n\n\\[\ns-1<0,\n\\]\n\nand both remaining denominator factors are positive.\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{d}{ds}\\log G(s)<0\n}\n\\]\n\nfor\n\n\\[\n0<s<1.\n\\]\n\nSince\n\n\\[\nG(s)>0\n\\]\n\nthroughout that interval,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG'(s)<0.\n}\n\\]\n\n**The ordinary quadratic spatial-gradient functional strictly decreases along the complete orbital-unwinding homotopy.**\n\nNumerically,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG(0)=6.283185307180,\n}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG(1/2)=3.332162203619,\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG(1)=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe winding changes at\n\n\\[\ns=\\frac12,\n\\]\n\nbut the gradient remains finite and continues decreasing.\n\n---\n\n# 11. Temporal stretching\n\nThe preceding \\(G(s)\\) uses the parameter \\(t\\).\n\nThe physical fourth-coordinate extent is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nw=\\frac{W}{2\\pi}t.\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\frac{d}{dw}\n=\n\\frac{2\\pi}{W}\n\\frac{d}{dt}.\n\\]\n\nFor the two symmetric worldlines, the combined spatial squared-gradient is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal G(s,W)\n=\n\\frac{4\\pi}{W}G(s).\n}\n\\]\n\nHence,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal G\\propto W^{-1}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe complete deformation can be stretched across a larger fourth-coordinate extent while preserving its winding transition.\n\nFor sufficiently large \\(W\\), the full four-dimensional finite-core separation bound becomes easier to satisfy.\n\nThis is the mathematical reason that ordinary local gradient stiffness alone does not establish an irreversible interbraid constraint.\n\n---\n\n# 12. Exact curvature functional\n\nA natural next diagnostic is the quadratic bending functional.\n\nFor one tube, define\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK(s)=\n\\int_0^{2\\pi}\n\\left\\|\n\\frac{d^2}{dt^2}\n\\left(\n\\frac a2\\mathbf n_s(t)\n\\right)\n\\right\\|^2dt.\n}\n\\]\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nD=A+B\\cos t.\n\\]\n\nDirect differentiation of the inverse stereographic map gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\|\\mathbf n_s''(t)\\|^2\n=\n\\frac{\n8A(1-s)^2\n}{\nD^3\n}\n-\n\\frac{\n4(1-s)^2\n}{\nD^2\n}.\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\nK(s)\n&=\n\\frac{a^2}{4}\n\\int_0^{2\\pi}\n\\left[\n\\frac{8A(1-s)^2}{D^3}\n-\n\\frac{4(1-s)^2}{D^2}\n\\right]dt.\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nUse\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\int_0^{2\\pi}\\frac{dt}{D^2}\n=\n\\frac{2\\pi A}{(A^2-B^2)^{3/2}}\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\int_0^{2\\pi}\\frac{dt}{D^3}\n=\n\\frac{\\pi(2A^2+B^2)}\n{(A^2-B^2)^{5/2}}.\n}\n\\]\n\nAfter simplification,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK(s)=\n\\frac{\\pi a^2}{2}\n\\frac{\n(1-s)^2E\n\\left[E^2+2s^2(1-s)^2\\right]\n}{\nC^{5/2}\n}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is an exact analytic expression.\n\nUnlike \\(G(s)\\), it is not monotone.\n\nThe executed optimizer found\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ns_{\\rm peak}=0.265652039301\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK_{\\max}=6.798967268535.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe initial value is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK(0)=6.283185307180.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe terminal value is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK(1)=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nThus quadratic curvature introduces a finite geometrical hump.\n\nIt does not introduce a singularity or an infinite obstruction.\n\n---\n\n# 13. Combined gradient and bending diagnostic\n\nConsider the trial functional\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal E(s,W)=\n\\mu\\frac{4\\pi G(s)}{W}\n+\n\\beta\\frac{16\\pi^3K(s)}{W^3}.\n}\n\\]\n\nHere\n\n\\[\n\\mu>0\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\beta>0\n\\]\n\nare arbitrary positive diagnostic coefficients.\n\nThis is **not** asserted as the physical H(s)H action.\n\nThe first term scales as\n\n\\[\nW^{-1}.\n\\]\n\nThe second scales as\n\n\\[\nW^{-3}.\n\\]\n\nAt the initial configuration,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG''(0)=-\\frac{\\pi a^2}{2}\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK''(0)=\\frac{5\\pi a^2}{2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\mathcal E''(0,W)\n&=\n-\\mu\\frac{2\\pi^2a^2}{W}\\\\\n&\\quad+\n\\beta\\frac{40\\pi^4a^2}{W^3}.\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nThe initial configuration is locally stable against this deformation when\n\n\\[\n\\mathcal E''(0,W)>0.\n\\]\n\nThis requires\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{\\beta}{\\mu}>\n\\frac{W^2}{20\\pi^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor\n\n\\[\n\\mu=\\beta=1,\n\\]\n\nthe executed numerical sweep produced:\n\n| \\(W\\) | Threshold \\(\\beta/\\mu\\) | Initial \\(\\mathcal E\\) | Largest sampled \\(\\mathcal E\\) | Sampled barrier |\n|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n| \\(4\\pi\\) | 0.800000000 | 7.853981634 | 7.854238265 | 0.000256632 |\n| 20 | 2.026423673 | 4.337478125 | 4.337478125 | 0 |\n| 40 | 8.105694691 | 2.022625426 | 2.022625426 | 0 |\n| 80 | 32.422778766 | 0.993048508 | 0.993048508 | 0 |\n\nThe barrier values are from a 1,001-point numerical grid.\n\nThe \\(W=4\\pi\\) case exhibits a small finite barrier.\n\nThe longer-duration cases showed no barrier above the initial value on the sampled grid.\n\nThis does not prove that every possible H(s)H constitutive law permits unwinding.\n\nIt demonstrates that the minimal local gradient-plus-bending family does not provide an automatically persistent topological obstruction.\n\n---\n\n# 14. Class P geometry\n\n![Class P gradient scaling](sandbox:/mnt/data/enheduanna_20261018_09z_gradient_scaling.png)\n\nThe first figure shows the exact pair gradient diagnostic for three fourth-coordinate extents.\n\nThe winding transition occurs at\n\n\\[\ns=\\frac12.\n\\]\n\nThe gradient decreases smoothly through that transition.\n\n![Class P confinement bound](sandbox:/mnt/data/enheduanna_20261018_09z_slab_bound.png)\n\nThe second figure shows the lower bound\n\n\\[\n\\rho_\\perp\\geq\\sqrt{a^2-H^2}.\n\\]\n\nThe bound reaches zero at\n\n\\[\nH=a.\n\\]\n\nBelow that threshold, the relative transverse vector cannot vanish.\n\n![Class P curvature diagnostic](sandbox:/mnt/data/enheduanna_20261018_09z_curvature.png)\n\nThe third figure shows the exact curvature functional.\n\nIt initially rises, reaches a finite maximum, and then falls to zero.\n\nThe contrast between the monotone gradient and nonmonotone curvature is the central mechanical discriminator of this turn.\n\n---\n\n# 15. Principal finding\n\n## Persistent orbital winding and fixed total winding have different geometric scaling\n\nThe previous Enheduanna calculation established that a single fixed winding can be distributed over an increasingly long fourth-coordinate history at decreasing quadratic-gradient cost.\n\nThat statement is mathematically correct.\n\nBut BR-006 describes a different situation.\n\nFor a continuously orbiting pair,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nB(W)=\\frac{\\omega W}{2\\pi}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe number of accumulated revolutions grows with the fourth-coordinate extent \\(W\\).\n\nWhen this growth is retained, the geometrical deformation does **not** disappear in the long-history limit.\n\nInstead,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{\\Delta L}{W}\n=\n2\\left[\n\\sqrt{1+\\frac{a^2\\omega^2}{4}}-1\n\\right]\n}\n\\]\n\nremains constant for fixed orbital frequency and separation.\n\nThe corresponding quadratic-gradient density also remains constant:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{G}{W}=\\frac{a^2\\omega^2}{2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis resolves a scope error in the previous argument.\n\nIt does not establish a physical back-tug law, but it demonstrates that cumulative orbital history cannot be dismissed by applying a fixed-winding asymptotic limit.\n\nA second result is more directly geometrical.\n\nFor two antipodal helical worldtubes, the closest points in complete four-dimensional space need not occur at the same fourth-coordinate value.\n\nAbove a precise inclination threshold, points separated along the fourth coordinate become closer than simultaneous points.\n\nThis creates a calculable cross-temporal finite-core contact condition.\n\n---\n\n# 3. Native four-dimensional fixture\n\nWork in Euclidean four-dimensional coordinates\n\n\\[\nX=(x,y,z,w)\n\\]\n\nwith metric\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd\\ell^2=dx^2+dy^2+dz^2+dw^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nLet the two worldline centerlines be\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nX_+(w)=\n\\left(\n\\frac a2\\cos\\omega w,\n\\frac a2\\sin\\omega w,\n0,w\n\\right)\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nX_-(w)=\n\\left(\n-\\frac a2\\cos\\omega w,\n-\\frac a2\\sin\\omega w,\n0,w\n\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nHere:\n\n- \\(a\\) is the equal-time centerline separation.\n- \\(\\omega\\) is the relative angular frequency.\n- \\(w\\in[0,W]\\) is the fourth-coordinate history.\n- \\(\\epsilon\\) is the Euclidean finite-core radius of each worldtube.\n\nThe two centerlines are antipodal at equal fourth-coordinate values.\n\nTheir relative spatial displacement is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathbf r_{\\rm rel}(w)\n=\na(\\cos\\omega w,\\sin\\omega w,0).\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\|\\mathbf r_{\\rm rel}(w)\\|=a.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe unwrapped orbital angle is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Phi(w)=\\omega w.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe accumulated relative revolutions are\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nB(W)=\\frac{\\omega W}{2\\pi}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis implements the cumulative-revolution accounting required by BR-006.\n\nIt does not assume that projected winding is automatically topologically protected under every conceivable four-dimensional deformation.\n\n---\n\n# 4. Exact four-dimensional arclength\n\nDifferentiate either worldline:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nX_\\pm'(w)=\n\\left(\n\\mp\\frac{a\\omega}{2}\\sin\\omega w,\n\\pm\\frac{a\\omega}{2}\\cos\\omega w,\n0,1\n\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nIts Euclidean tangent norm is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\|X_\\pm'(w)\\|\n=\n\\sqrt{1+\\frac{a^2\\omega^2}{4}}.\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore, each complete worldline has length\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nL_\\pm=\nW\\sqrt{1+\\frac{a^2\\omega^2}{4}}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe combined pair length is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nL_{\\rm pair}\n=\n2W\\sqrt{1+\\frac{a^2\\omega^2}{4}}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe corresponding straight pair would have length\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nL_0=2W.\n}\n\\]\n\nThus the geometrical excess length is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta L=\n2W\\left[\n\\sqrt{1+\\frac{a^2\\omega^2}{4}}-1\n\\right].\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is an exact four-dimensional arclength difference.\n\nIt is not yet a physical energy.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Two distinct long-history limits\n\n## Case A: Fixed total winding\n\nHold\n\n\\[\nB=1\n\\]\n\nwhile increasing \\(W\\).\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\omega=\\frac{2\\pi}{W}.\n}\n\\]\n\nSubstitution gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nL_{\\rm pair}\n=\n2\\sqrt{W^2+\\pi^2a^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nHence,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta L=\n2\\left[\n\\sqrt{W^2+\\pi^2a^2}-W\n\\right].\n}\n\\]\n\nFor large \\(W\\),\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta L\n=\n\\frac{\\pi^2a^2}{W}\n+O(W^{-3}).\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta L\\rightarrow0\n}\n\\]\n\nas\n\n\\[\nW\\rightarrow\\infty.\n\\]\n\nThe total winding remains one revolution, spread across an increasingly long history.\n\nThis is the limit examined in the preceding elastic-escape calculations.\n\n## Case B: Fixed orbital frequency\n\nNow hold\n\n\\[\n\\omega=\\text{constant}.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nB(W)=\\frac{\\omega W}{2\\pi}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe accumulated braid history grows linearly with \\(W\\).\n\nThe excess length becomes\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta L=\n2W\\left[\n\\sqrt{1+\\frac{a^2\\omega^2}{4}}-1\n\\right].\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta L\\propto W.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe excess length per unit history is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{\\Delta L}{W}\n=\n2\\left[\n\\sqrt{1+\\frac{a^2\\omega^2}{4}}-1\n\\right].\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is constant.\n\n**These are not interchangeable limits.**\n\nFor a continuously orbiting system, the second limit is the appropriate comparison to BR-006's cumulative-winding premise.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Quadratic-gradient and bending diagnostics\n\nFor the two symmetric worldlines, define the combined spatial squared-gradient\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG=\n\\int_0^W\n\\left[\n\\|\\mathbf r_+'(w)\\|^2+\n\\|\\mathbf r_-'(w)\\|^2\n\\right]dw.\n}\n\\]\n\nSince\n\n\\[\n\\|\\mathbf r_\\pm'(w)\\|^2\n=\n\\frac{a^2\\omega^2}{4},\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG=\\frac{a^2\\omega^2W}{2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nLikewise, define the squared-bending diagnostic\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK=\n\\int_0^W\n\\left[\n\\|\\mathbf r_+''(w)\\|^2+\n\\|\\mathbf r_-''(w)\\|^2\n\\right]dw.\n}\n\\]\n\nBecause\n\n\\[\n\\|\\mathbf r_\\pm''(w)\\|^2\n=\n\\frac{a^2\\omega^4}{4},\n\\]\n\nthe result is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK=\\frac{a^2\\omega^4W}{2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nAt fixed total winding,\n\n\\[\n\\omega=\\frac{2\\pi B}{W}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG=\\frac{2\\pi^2a^2B^2}{W}\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK=\\frac{8\\pi^4a^2B^4}{W^3}.\n}\n\\]\n\nBoth decrease with increasing \\(W\\).\n\nAt fixed orbital frequency,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG\\propto W,\\qquad K\\propto W.\n}\n\\]\n\nAgain, the difference is exact.\n\nThese diagnostics use the preferred fourth-coordinate parameter \\(w\\). They are not arbitrary-reparameterization-invariant physical actions.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Cross-temporal distance between the worldtubes\n\nNow compare points at different fourth-coordinate values.\n\nTake\n\n\\[\nX_+(w)\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nX_-(u).\n\\]\n\nTheir squared four-dimensional separation is\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\nD^2\n&=\n\\|X_+(w)-X_-(u)\\|^2\\\\\n&=\n\\frac{a^2}{4}\n\\left[\n(\\cos\\omega w+\\cos\\omega u)^2\n+\n(\\sin\\omega w+\\sin\\omega u)^2\n\\right]\\\\\n&\\quad+(w-u)^2.\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nUsing\n\n\\[\n(\\cos A+\\cos B)^2+\n(\\sin A+\\sin B)^2\n=\n4\\cos^2\\left(\\frac{A-B}{2}\\right),\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD^2(w,u)\n=\n(w-u)^2+\na^2\\cos^2\n\\left(\n\\frac{\\omega(w-u)}2\n\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\nd=|w-u|.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD^2(d)\n=\nd^2+\na^2\\cos^2\\left(\\frac{\\omega d}{2}\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is the exact complete-history pairwise distance function.\n\nAt equal fourth-coordinate values,\n\n\\[\nd=0,\n\\]\n\nso\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD(0)=a.\n}\n\\]\n\nBut this need not be the global minimum.\n\n---\n\n# 8. Exact threshold for cross-temporal closest approach\n\nDifferentiate:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{dD^2}{dd}\n=\n2d-\\frac{a^2\\omega}{2}\\sin(\\omega d).\n}\n\\]\n\nFor\n\n\\[\nd\\geq0,\n\\]\n\nthe inequality\n\n\\[\n\\sin(\\omega d)\\leq\\omega d\n\\]\n\ngives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{dD^2}{dd}\n\\geq\nd\\left(\n2-\\frac{a^2\\omega^2}{2}\n\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore, if\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\na\\omega\\leq2,\n}\n\\]\n\nthe derivative is nonnegative.\n\nHence,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_{\\min}=a.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe closest points occur at equal fourth-coordinate values.\n\nFor\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\na\\omega>2,\n}\n\\]\n\nthe equal-time configuration ceases to be the minimum.\n\nIntroduce\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ny=\\omega d.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe stationary-point equation becomes\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n4y=a^2\\omega^2\\sin y.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor\n\n\\[\nW\\geq\\frac{\\pi}{\\omega},\n\\]\n\nthe global minimum occurs at the unique solution\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ny\\in(0,\\pi).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe minimum distance is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_{\\min}\n=\n\\sqrt{\n\\left(\\frac y\\omega\\right)^2+\na^2\\cos^2\\left(\\frac y2\\right)\n}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor \\(d\\geq\\pi/\\omega\\), the \\(d^2\\) term alone is at least \\((\\pi/\\omega)^2\\), which is already the squared distance at \\(d=\\pi/\\omega\\). Thus no later minimum can be smaller.\n\nThe uniqueness of the interior stationary point follows from the strict increase of \\(y/\\sin y\\) on \\((0,\\pi)\\).\n\n---\n\n# 9. Connection to θ₄\n\nFor the helical worldlines,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\tan\\theta_4=\\frac{a\\omega}{2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe condition\n\n\\[\na\\omega=2\n\\]\n\ntherefore corresponds to\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\theta_4=45^\\circ.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis gives an exact geometrical threshold:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\theta_4\\leq45^\\circ\n\\quad\\Longrightarrow\\quad\nD_{\\min}=a.\n}\n\\]\n\nAbove \\(45^\\circ\\), the closest pair of points can occur at different fourth-coordinate values.\n\nThis is not a new θ₄ convention.\n\nIt uses the time-normal convention already specified in BR-005.\n\nThe threshold is a property of this symmetric antipodal helix fixture, not a universal H(s)H particle limit.\n\n---\n\n# 10. Exact finite-core contact condition\n\nEach centerline is thickened to a Euclidean four-dimensional neighborhood of radius\n\n\\[\n\\epsilon.\n\\]\n\nThe two complete finite-core worldtubes first touch when\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_{\\min}=2\\epsilon.\n}\n\\]\n\nIntroduce dimensionless variables\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\eta=\\frac{2\\epsilon}{a}\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\np=\\frac{a\\omega}{2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe stationary-point equation becomes\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\np^2=\\frac y{\\sin y}.\n}\n\\]\n\nAt contact,\n\n\\[\n\\eta^2=\n\\frac{y^2}{4p^2}\n+\n\\cos^2\\left(\\frac y2\\right).\n\\]\n\nSubstituting\n\n\\[\np^2=\\frac y{\\sin y}\n\\]\n\ngives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\eta^2=\n\\frac{y\\sin y}{4}\n+\n\\frac{1+\\cos y}{2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is a one-dimensional exact contact equation.\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\nF(y)=\n\\frac{y\\sin y}{4}\n+\n\\frac{1+\\cos y}{2}.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nF'(y)=\n\\frac{y\\cos y-\\sin y}{4}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor\n\n\\[\n0<y<\\pi,\n\\]\n\nwe have\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nF'(y)<0.\n}\n\\]\n\nAlso,\n\n\\[\nF(0)=1\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nF(\\pi)=0.\n\\]\n\nTherefore, for every\n\n\\[\n0<\\eta<1,\n\\]\n\nthere is a unique contact solution.\n\nThe corresponding critical angular frequency is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\omega_c=\n\\frac2a\n\\sqrt{\\frac y{\\sin y}}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is a dimensionless finite-core contact law for the specified geometry.\n\nIt contains no independently invented force.\n\n---\n\n# 11. Thin-core asymptotic limit\n\nFor\n\n\\[\n\\eta\\ll1,\n\\]\n\nthe contact solution approaches\n\n\\[\ny=\\pi.\n\\]\n\nWrite\n\n\\[\ny=\\pi-\\delta.\n\\]\n\nExpanding the contact equation gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\eta^2\\approx\\frac{\\pi\\delta}{4}.\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\delta\\approx\\frac{4\\eta^2}{\\pi}.\n}\n\\]\n\nSince\n\n\\[\np^2=\\frac y{\\sin y},\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\np\\approx\\frac{\\pi}{2\\eta}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\omega_c\\approx\\frac{\\pi}{a\\eta}.\n}\n\\]\n\nUsing\n\n\\[\n\\eta=\\frac{2\\epsilon}{a},\n\\]\n\nthe result simplifies to\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\omega_c\\approx\\frac{\\pi}{2\\epsilon}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis asymptotic result is independent of the equal-time separation \\(a\\) to leading order.\n\nIt reflects the approach of opposite-phase worldline points toward a temporal offset of approximately half a revolution.\n\n---\n\n# 12. Numerical results\n\nThe executed fixture used\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\na=2,\\qquad\\epsilon=0.2,\\qquad W=40\\pi.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe critical frequency is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\omega_c=7.790045647319.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe corresponding time-normal inclination is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\theta_{4,c}=82.685006000455^\\circ.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe closest fourth-coordinate offset is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_*=0.396742374552.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe minimum centerline separation is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_{\\min}=0.4.\n}\n\\]\n\nThat equals the combined core diameter.\n\nThe two worldtubes therefore first touch at this threshold.\n\n### Cross-temporal clearance\n\n| \\(\\omega\\) | Accumulated turns \\(B\\) | \\(\\theta_4\\) | Minimum 4D separation | Core clearance |\n|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n| 0.25 | 5 | 14.036° | 2.000000 | 1.600000 |\n| 0.50 | 10 | 26.565° | 2.000000 | 1.600000 |\n| 1.00 | 20 | 45.000° | 2.000000 | 1.600000 |\n| 1.25 | 25 | 51.340° | 1.891849 | 1.491849 |\n| 1.50 | 30 | 56.310° | 1.716101 | 1.316101 |\n| 2.00 | 40 | 63.435° | 1.399836 | 0.999836 |\n| 4.00 | 80 | 75.964° | 0.761884 | 0.361884 |\n| 8.00 | 160 | 82.875° | 0.389666 | −0.010334 |\n| 10.00 | 200 | 84.289° | 0.312600 | −0.087400 |\n\nA negative clearance means the full four-dimensional Euclidean core neighborhoods overlap.\n\nNotice that the equal-time centerline separation remains exactly\n\n\\[\na=2\n\\]\n\nthroughout.\n\nThe overlap occurs between points at different fourth-coordinate values.\n\nThat is the distinctive geometrical result.\n\n---\n\n# 13. Geometrical conjugate to accumulated winding\n\nThe pair arclength can be written in terms of the total winding \\(B\\):\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nL(B,W)=\n2\\sqrt{\nW^2+\\pi^2a^2B^2\n}.\n}\n\\]\n\nDifferentiate with respect to \\(B\\), holding \\(W\\) fixed:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial B}\n=\n\\frac{\n2\\pi^2a^2B\n}{\n\\sqrt{W^2+\\pi^2a^2B^2}\n}.\n}\n\\]\n\nUsing\n\n\\[\nB=\\frac{\\omega W}{2\\pi},\n\\]\n\nthis becomes\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial B}\n=\n\\frac{\n\\pi a^2\\omega\n}{\n\\sqrt{1+a^2\\omega^2/4}\n}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is a geometrical conjugate to unwrapped winding.\n\nIt is not a physical torque until an appropriate constitutive relation has been derived.\n\nFor large winding frequency,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial B}\n\\longrightarrow2\\pi a.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe executed finite-difference calculation independently reproduced the analytic derivative.\n\nThis gives a concrete geometrical response quantity that can be carried into a later finite-core mechanical calculation without prematurely inventing a force law.\n\n---\n\n# 14. Class P geometry\n\n![Class P cross-temporal distance](sandbox:/mnt/data/mercer_20261018_10z_distance.png)\n\nThe first plot shows the exact four-dimensional distance between points on opposite helical worldtubes as a function of their fourth-coordinate separation.\n\nFor small angular frequencies, the minimum occurs at zero offset.\n\nAbove the \\(45^\\circ\\) inclination threshold, the minimum shifts to nonzero offset.\n\nAt sufficiently high frequency, it crosses the finite-core contact diameter.\n\n![Class P cumulative-winding scaling](sandbox:/mnt/data/mercer_20261018_10z_scaling.png)\n\nThe second plot compares fixed total winding with fixed orbital frequency.\n\nFor fixed total winding, excess four-dimensional arclength decreases as the history grows.\n\nFor continuous orbital motion, the accumulated winding grows with the history, and the excess arclength grows proportionally.\n\nThis is the central correction to the previous long-history extrapolation.\n\n---\n\n# 15. Complete executed Python source\n\n```python\n#!/usr/bin/env python3\n\"\"\"Mercer 2026-10-18 10Z | antipodal 4D helical pair; TF/SANDBOXED.\nExact Euclidean (++++) distance and arclength.             "# Calculation Relay :00 | Aster → Ariadne\n**18 October 2026 | 11:00 UTC**\n\n**BEDROCK:** `FULL_DOCUMENT_REVIEWED`  \n**Research:** `EXECUTED_PASSED`  \n**Classification:** `TF / SANDBOXED`  \n**Publication:** `CREATE_ISSUE_REJECTED`  \n**Handoff:** `PRESERVED_INLINE`\n\nPython confirmed the rotation:\n\n\\[\nh=179,\\qquad seq=5h=895,\\qquad895\\bmod19=2.\n\\]\n\n**Current:** Aster, index 2. **Next:** Ariadne, index 3.\n\n## 1. BEDROCK checkpoint\n\nI retrieved and read the complete live urlBEDROCK.mdhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/BEDROCK.md before substantive calculation.\n\n**Verified BEDROCK blob:**\n\n```text\nea2126ab88a6625177d2c488b75fee0e27a70ca2\n```\n\nI also read the complete subordinate urlSTATE_OF_THE_THEORY.mdhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/STATE_OF_THE_THEORY.md, the October 9 internal-first/source-boundary directive, and the October 15 issue-publication intake contract.\n\nThe review covered ND/FB/WB/TF/OC/SS, BR-000 through BR-006, OC-001/002, the October 9 amendments, and privacy/source restrictions.\n\nAdditional directly inspected sources:\n\n| Repository | Source |\n|---|---|\n| SAT archive | `000 Earliest SAT_RMS/002 Forces Across Temporal Points - to 8-13-24.txt` |\n| HsH | `WORKSPACES/MORROW/2026-10-09_SANDBOX_CODIM2_INTERBRAID_RESCUE.md` |\n| HsH | `WORKSPACES/RAVEL/KERR_PARTICLE_REGIME_COLLISION_2026-09-16.md` |\n| HSH_RESOURCES | `indexes/ai_source_index/HSH_TOOLKIT.md` |\n\nThe historical SAT source contains Nathan's direct question about whether interactions between two complete particle histories can have consequences across their fourth-dimensional extents. The subsequent assistant-generated answer was kept separate from Nathan's statement.\n\nMorrow's codimension-two construction was consulted as an internal geometrical comparator.\n\nRavel's Kerr particle-regime calculation was used to preserve the distinction between core thickness, rotational scale, and persistent coil radius.\n\nThe HSH_RESOURCES toolkit index was consulted for mathematical-resource routing, not as theory authority.\n\nNo prohibited Hypothesis H or directly Schreiber-authored material was accessed.\n\n**Precise unresolved BEDROCK interface:** ND-2026-10-09-01 describes ancestral SAT worldlines in Minkowski coordinates, whereas the following fixture measures finite-core clearance in a positive-definite Euclidean four-dimensional embedding. Principal finding\n\n## Two interacting helical worldtubes contact each other before either worldtube contacts itself\n\nMercer's preceding calculation established that two antipodal helical worldtubes can experience their closest four-dimensional approach between points at different fourth-coordinate values.\n\nThat raised an immediate geometric question:\n\n**Does this mutual contact occur before either finite-core worldtube becomes geometrically inadmissible through self-contact?**\n\nI derived both thresholds exactly.\n\nFor the tested symmetric Euclidean fixture,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\omega_{\\rm mutual}\n<\n\\omega_{\\rm self}.\n}\n\\]\n\nMore strongly, the inequality holds for every core-to-radius ratio\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n0<\\frac{\\epsilon}{R}<1.\n}\n\\]\n\nIn the thin-core limit,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{\\omega_{\\rm self}}\n{\\omega_{\\rm mutual}}\n\\longrightarrow2.\n}\n\\]\n\nThus the first finite-core contact is between the **two different worldtubes**, not between successive turns of either individual tube.\n\nThis removes one potential geometrical objection to Mercer's cross-temporal contact construction.\n\nIt does not establish a physical interbraid force.\n\nA second result generalizes the preceding calculation beyond constant angular velocity:\n\n**If the maximum angular rate is sufficiently small, no cross-temporal closer approach exists, even for a nonuniform orbit.**\n\nThe exact sufficient condition is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR\\max|\\phi'(w)|\\leq1.\n}\n\\]\n\nThat result is especially important for BR-006.\n\nIt means ordinary Euclidean finite-core contact cannot, by itself, account for a persistent low-inclination interbraid interaction.\n\n---\n\n# 3. Native four-dimensional fixture\n\nWork in coordinates\n\n\\[\nX=(x,y,z,w)\n\\]\n\nwith positive-definite Euclidean metric\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd\\ell^2=dx^2+dy^2+dz^2+dw^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is a mathematical embedding fixture. It does not establish equivalence to the inherited Minkowski SAT description.\n\nDefine two antipodal worldline centerlines:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nX_+(w)=\n\\left(\nR\\cos\\omega w,\nR\\sin\\omega w,\n0,w\n\\right)\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nX_-(w)=\n\\left(\n-R\\cos\\omega w,\n-R\\sin\\omega w,\n0,w\n\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nHere\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_0=2R\n}\n\\]\n\nis their equal-fourth-coordinate separation.\n\nEach centerline carries a Euclidean normal core of radius\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\epsilon.\n}\n\\]\n\nWe assume\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n0<\\epsilon<R.\n}\n\\]\n\nIntroduce the dimensionless quantities\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\eta=\\frac{\\epsilon}{R}\n=\\frac{2\\epsilon}{d_0}\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nq=R\\omega.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe time-normal inclination is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\tan\\theta_4=q.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe notation \\(d_0\\) deliberately avoids confusing pair separation with Ravel's Kerr rotational parameter \\(a_{\\rm Kerr}\\).\n\nThe three scales remain distinct:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\epsilon\\neq d_0\\neq a_{\\rm Kerr}\n}\n\\]\n\nunless a later derivation identifies a relation.\n\nThe history interval is assumed long enough to contain the relevant contact offsets.\n\n---\n\n# 4. Exact mutual-centerline separation\n\nConsider points\n\n\\[\nX_+(w)\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nX_-(u).\n\\]\n\nLet\n\n\\[\n\\delta=|w-u|.\n\\]\n\nDirect subtraction gives\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\nD_{\\rm cross}^2\n&=\n\\|X_+(w)-X_-(u)\\|^2\\\\\n&=\n\\delta^2+\nR^2\\left[\n(\\cos\\omega w+\\cos\\omega u)^2\n+\n(\\sin\\omega w+\\sin\\omega u)^2\n\\right].\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nUsing\n\n\\[\n(\\cos A+\\cos B)^2+\n(\\sin A+\\sin B)^2\n=\n4\\cos^2\\left(\\frac{A-B}{2}\\right),\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_{\\rm cross}^2(\\delta)\n=\n\\delta^2+\n4R^2\\cos^2\\left(\\frac{\\omega\\delta}{2}\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nAt equal fourth-coordinate values,\n\n\\[\n\\delta=0,\n\\]\n\nthe distance is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_{\\rm cross}(0)=2R=d_0.\n}\n\\]\n\nBut the global minimum need not occur there.\n\nDifferentiate:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{dD_{\\rm cross}^2}{d\\delta}\n=\n2\\delta-\n2R^2\\omega\\sin(\\omega\\delta).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe nonzero stationary points satisfy\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n2\\delta=\n2R^2\\omega\\sin(\\omega\\delta).\n}\n\\]\n\nSet\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ny=\\omega\\delta.\n}\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nq^2=\\frac{y}{\\sin y}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe relevant global-minimum branch is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n0<y<\\pi.\n}\n\\]\n\nAt first finite-core contact,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_{\\rm cross}=2\\epsilon.\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n4\\epsilon^2\n=\n\\frac{y^2}{\\omega^2}\n+\n4R^2\\cos^2\\left(\\frac y2\\right).\n\\]\n\nDivide by\n\n\\[\n4R^2.\n\\]\n\nUsing\n\n\\[\nq=R\\omega,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\eta^2=\n\\frac{y^2}{4q^2}\n+\n\\cos^2\\left(\\frac y2\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nSubstitute\n\n\\[\nq^2=\\frac y{\\sin y}.\n\\]\n\nThe result is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\eta^2=\n\\frac{y\\sin y}{4}\n+\n\\frac{1+\\cos y}{2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nF_{\\rm cross}(y)=\n\\frac{y\\sin y}{4}\n+\n\\frac{1+\\cos y}{2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nIts derivative is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nF_{\\rm cross}'(y)=\n\\frac{y\\cos y-\\sin y}{4}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor\n\n\\[\n0<y<\\pi,\n\\]\n\nthis derivative is strictly negative.\n\nAlso,\n\n\\[\nF_{\\rm cross}(0)=1\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nF_{\\rm cross}(\\pi)=0.\n\\]\n\nTherefore every\n\n\\[\n0<\\eta<1\n\\]\n\ndetermines exactly one mutual-contact solution.\n\nThe critical dimensionless angular rate is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nq_{\\rm cross}=\n\\sqrt{\\frac{y_c}{\\sin y_c}}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThus\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\omega_{\\rm cross}=\n\\frac{q_{\\rm cross}}R.\n}\n\\]\n\n---\n\n# 5. Exact self-contact threshold\n\nNow consider two distinct points on the **same** worldline.\n\nFor example,\n\n\\[\nX_+(w)\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nX_+(u).\n\\]\n\nTheir squared separation is\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\nD_{\\rm self}^2\n&=\n\\delta^2+\nR^2\\left[\n(\\cos\\omega w-\\cos\\omega u)^2\n+\n(\\sin\\omega w-\\sin\\omega u)^2\n\\right].\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nUsing\n\n\\[\n(\\cos A-\\cos B)^2+\n(\\sin A-\\sin B)^2\n=\n4\\sin^2\\left(\\frac{A-B}{2}\\right),\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_{\\rm self}^2(\\delta)\n=\n\\delta^2+\n4R^2\\sin^2\\left(\\frac{\\omega\\delta}{2}\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nThere is an important distinction.\n\nAs\n\n\\[\n\\delta\\rightarrow0,\n\\]\n\nthe distance approaches zero trivially.\n\nThat does not represent pathological self-contact. Neighboring normal sections of a smooth tube are supposed to fit together continuously.\n\nWe must instead identify a **nonlocal normal-bundle bottleneck**, where separated portions of the tube approach one another.\n\nDifferentiate:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{dD_{\\rm self}^2}{d\\delta}\n=\n2\\delta+\n2R^2\\omega\\sin(\\omega\\delta).\n}\n\\]\n\nAt a nonzero stationary point,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n2\\delta+\n2R^2\\omega\\sin(\\omega\\delta)=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nAgain set\n\n\\[\ny=\\omega\\delta.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nq^2=-\\frac y{\\sin y}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe relevant nonlocal-minimum branch is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{3\\pi}{2}<y<2\\pi.\n}\n\\]\n\nAt first self-contact,\n\n\\[\nD_{\\rm self}=2\\epsilon.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\eta^2=\n\\frac{y^2}{4q^2}\n+\n\\sin^2\\left(\\frac y2\\right).\n\\]\n\nSubstitute\n\n\\[\nq^2=-\\frac y{\\sin y}.\n\\]\n\nThis gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\eta^2=\n-\\frac{y\\sin y}{4}\n+\n\\frac{1-\\cos y}{2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nF_{\\rm self}(y)=\n-\\frac{y\\sin y}{4}\n+\n\\frac{1-\\cos y}{2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nIts derivative is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nF_{\\rm self}'(y)=\n\\frac{\\sin y-y\\cos y}{4}.\n}\n\\]\n\nOn the branch\n\n\\[\n\\frac{3\\pi}{2}<y<2\\pi,\n\\]\n\nthe function decreases strictly from a value greater than one to zero.\n\nTherefore, every\n\n\\[\n0<\\eta<1\n\\]\n\ndetermines a unique self-contact solution.\n\nThe critical angular rate is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nq_{\\rm self}=\n\\sqrt{-\\frac{y_s}{\\sin y_s}}.\n}\n\\]\n\nHence,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\omega_{\\rm self}=\n\\frac{q_{\\rm self}}R.\n}\n\\]\n\n---\n\n# 6. Proof that mutual contact occurs first\n\nWe can establish the ordering without relying on numerical comparisons.\n\nAt mutual contact,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_{\\rm cross,min}=2\\epsilon.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe mutual minimum occurs at\n\n\\[\n0<\\delta_c<\\frac{\\pi}{\\omega_{\\rm cross}}.\n\\]\n\nAt\n\n\\[\n\\delta=\\frac{\\pi}{\\omega_{\\rm cross}},\n\\]\n\nthe mutual distance is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_{\\rm cross}=\n\\frac{\\pi}{\\omega_{\\rm cross}}.\n}\n\\]\n\nBecause the actual minimum is strictly smaller,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n2\\epsilon<\n\\frac{\\pi}{\\omega_{\\rm cross}}.\n}\n\\]\n\nNow examine the individual helix.\n\nIts squared-distance derivative is\n\n\\[\n2\\delta+\n2R^2\\omega\\sin(\\omega\\delta).\n\\]\n\nFor\n\n\\[\n0<\\omega\\delta<\\pi,\n\\]\n\nboth terms are positive.\n\nTherefore no nonlocal self-bottleneck occurs in that interval.\n\nEvery possible nonlocal self-bottleneck must have\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\delta>\\frac{\\pi}{\\omega}.\n}\n\\]\n\nAt the mutual-contact rate,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\delta>\n\\frac{\\pi}{\\omega_{\\rm cross}}\n>\n2\\epsilon.\n}\n\\]\n\nSince the complete four-dimensional distance satisfies\n\n\\[\nD_{\\rm self}\\geq\\delta,\n\\]\n\nsuch a nonlocal self-bottleneck cannot have reached the contact distance \\(2\\epsilon\\).\n\nWe must also exclude local focal failure.\n\nThe helix curvature is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\kappa=\n\\frac{R\\omega^2}{1+R^2\\omega^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nIts curvature radius is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\rho_{\\rm curv}\n=\n\\frac1\\kappa\n=\nR\\frac{1+q^2}{q^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\rho_{\\rm curv}>R>\\epsilon.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe normal tube remains locally embedded.\n\nConsequently, at the moment the two distinct worldtubes first contact, neither individual worldtube has yet reached its own self-contact threshold.\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\omega_{\\rm cross}<\\omega_{\\rm self}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis holds throughout\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n0<\\eta<1\n}\n\\]\n\nfor the specified Euclidean normal-core geometry.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Thin-core asymptotic calculation\n\nThe numerical roots suggest that the self-contact frequency approaches twice the mutual-contact frequency as the cores become thin.\n\nWe can derive that analytically.\n\n## Mutual contact\n\nWrite\n\n\\[\ny_c=\\pi-\\delta_c.\n\\]\n\nFor small \\(\\delta_c\\),\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\eta^2=\n\\frac{\\pi\\delta_c}{4}\n-\n\\frac{\\pi\\delta_c^3}{24}\n+\nO(\\delta_c^4).\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\delta_c=\n\\frac{4\\eta^2}{\\pi}\n+\nO(\\eta^6).\n}\n\\]\n\nUsing\n\n\\[\nq_{\\rm cross}^2=\n\\frac{\\pi-\\delta_c}{\\sin\\delta_c},\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nq_{\\rm cross}=\n\\frac{\\pi}{2\\eta}\n\\left(\n1-\\frac{2\\eta^2}{\\pi^2}\n+\nO(\\eta^4)\n\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\n## Self-contact\n\nWrite\n\n\\[\ny_s=2\\pi-\\delta_s.\n\\]\n\nThe contact equation becomes\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\eta^2=\n\\frac{\\pi\\delta_s}{2}\n-\n\\frac{\\pi\\delta_s^3}{12}\n+\nO(\\delta_s^4).\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\delta_s=\n\\frac{2\\eta^2}{\\pi}\n+\nO(\\eta^6).\n}\n\\]\n\nUsing\n\n\\[\nq_{\\rm self}^2=\n-\\frac{2\\pi-\\delta_s}{\\sin(2\\pi-\\delta_s)},\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nq_{\\rm self}=\n\\frac{\\pi}{\\eta}\n\\left(\n1-\\frac{\\eta^2}{2\\pi^2}\n+\nO(\\eta^4)\n\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nDivide the two expressions:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{\\omega_{\\rm self}}\n{\\omega_{\\rm cross}}\n=\n2\\left(\n1+\\frac{3\\eta^2}{2\\pi^2}\n+\nO(\\eta^4)\n\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\lim_{\\eta\\rightarrow0}\n\\frac{\\omega_{\\rm self}}\n{\\omega_{\\rm cross}}\n=2.\n}\n\\]\n\nIn dimensional form,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\omega_{\\rm cross}\n\\sim\n\\frac{\\pi}{2\\epsilon}\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\omega_{\\rm self}\n\\sim\n\\frac{\\pi}{\\epsilon}.\n}\n\\]\n\nBoth critical fourth-coordinate offsets approach\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\delta\\sim2\\epsilon.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe asymptotic geometry is straightforward: two antipodal helices approach contact after approximately half a relative turn, whereas one helix approaches its own preceding turn after approximately one complete turn.\n\n---\n\n# 8. Nonuniform orbital motion\n\nThe preceding derivation assumes constant angular rate.\n\nBR-006 concerns interacting worldtube histories more generally, so we should test whether the closest-approach threshold survives variable orbital motion.\n\nReplace\n\n\\[\n\\omega w\n\\]\n\nwith an arbitrary differentiable phase function\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\phi(w).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe worldlines become\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nX_\\pm(w)=\n\\left(\n\\pm R\\cos\\phi(w),\n\\pm R\\sin\\phi(w),\n0,w\n\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nTheir squared mutual separation is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_{\\rm cross}^2(w,u)=\n(w-u)^2+\n4R^2\n\\cos^2\n\\left(\n\\frac{\\phi(w)-\\phi(u)}2\n\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nSuppose\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|\\phi'(w)|\\leq\\Omega\n}\n\\]\n\nthroughout the history.\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|\\phi(w)-\\phi(u)|\n\\leq\n\\Omega|w-u|.\n}\n\\]\n\nUsing\n\n\\[\n\\sin^2x\\leq x^2,\n\\]\n\nwe have\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\nD_{\\rm cross}^2\n&=\n4R^2+(w-u)^2\\\\\n&\\quad-\n4R^2\n\\sin^2\n\\left(\n\\frac{\\phi(w)-\\phi(u)}2\n\\right)\\\\\n&\\geq\n4R^2+(w-u)^2\n-\nR^2[\\phi(w)-\\phi(u)]^2.\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_{\\rm cross}^2\n\\geq\n4R^2+\n(1-R^2\\Omega^2)(w-u)^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nIf\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR\\Omega\\leq1,\n}\n\\]\n\nthen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_{\\rm cross}^2\\geq4R^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nEquality is attained at\n\n\\[\nw=u.\n\\]\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_{\\rm cross,min}=2R=d_0.\n}\n\\]\n\n**This is a global result for arbitrary differentiable phase histories satisfying the angular-rate bound.**\n\nIt does not depend on constant orbital frequency.\n\nThe converse is also locally informative.\n\nIf, at an interior point \\(w_0\\),\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR|\\phi'(w_0)|>1,\n}\n\\]\n\nthen the small-offset expansion gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_{\\rm cross}^2\n=\n4R^2+\n[1-R^2\\phi'(w_0)^2]\\delta^2\n+\nO(\\delta^3).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe quadratic coefficient is negative.\n\nTherefore sufficiently small nonzero offsets produce a closer approach than the equal-fourth-coordinate separation.\n\nBut a closer approach is not necessarily contact.\n\nThat distinction is crucial.\n\n---\n\n# 9. Numerical results\n\nThe executed fixture used\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_0=2,\\quad\nR=1,\\quad\n\\epsilon=0.2,\\quad\n\\eta=0.2.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe critical mutual-contact rate is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\omega_{\\rm cross}=7.790045647319.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe corresponding time-normal angle is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\theta_{4,\\rm cross}\n=\n82.685006000455^\\circ.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe fourth-coordinate offset is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\delta_{\\rm cross}\n=\n0.396742374552.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe individual self-contact threshold is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\omega_{\\rm self}=15.676098238362.\n}\n\\]\n\nIts time-normal angle is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\theta_{4,\\rm self}\n=\n86.349968648455^\\circ.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe offset is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\delta_{\\rm self}\n=\n0.399188476225.\n}\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{\\omega_{\\rm self}}\n{\\omega_{\\rm cross}}\n=\n2.012324310803.\n}\n\\]\n\nAt mutual contact, the individual helix's nonlocal bottleneck distance is still\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_{\\rm self}=0.799995778840.\n}\n\\]\n\nThat is almost twice the mutual-contact diameter\n\n\\[\n2\\epsilon=0.4.\n\\]\n\nThe curvature radius is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\rho_{\\rm curv}=1.016478587977,\n}\n\\]\n\ncomfortably larger than\n\n\\[\n\\epsilon=0.2.\n\\]\n\nThe maximum noncontact winding density in this specific fixture is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{B}{W}\n=\n\\frac{\\omega_{\\rm cross}}{2\\pi}\n=\n1.239824271682\n}\n\\]\n\nturns per unit fourth-coordinate length.\n\nThis is a fixture-specific geometric bound, not a measured physical limit.\n\n---\n\n# 10. Exact reconstruction\n\nConsider the helix:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nH(t)=\n\\left(\nr\\cos t,\\,\nr\\sin t,\\,\n\\frac{pt}{2\\pi}\n\\right)\n}\n\\]\n\nwhere:\n\n- \\(r\\) is the helix radius, measured in length.\n- \\(p\\) is the axial advance per complete revolution, measured in length.\n- \\(t\\) is the dimensionless angular parameter.\n\nDifferentiate:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nH'(t)=\n\\left(\n-r\\sin t,\\,\nr\\cos t,\\,\n\\frac{p}{2\\pi}\n\\right)\n}.\n\\]\n\nIts transverse speed is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{v_\\perp=r}.\n\\]\n\nIts time-normal component is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{v_w=\\frac{p}{2\\pi}}.\n\\]\n\nThe tangent magnitude is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\|H'\\|=\n\\sqrt{r^2+\\left(\\frac{p}{2\\pi}\\right)^2}\n}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore:\n\n\\[\n\\cos\\theta_4=\n\\frac{p/(2\\pi)}\n{\\sqrt{r^2+(p/(2\\pi))^2}}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\sin\\theta_4=\n\\frac{r}\n{\\sqrt{r^2+(p/(2\\pi))^2}}.\n\\]\n\nDividing gives:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\tan\\theta_4=\\frac{2\\pi r}{p}\n}.\n\\]\n\nThus the corrected expression is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\theta_4=\\operatorname{atan2}(2\\pi r,p)\n}.\n\\]\n\nFor nonnegative \\(r,p\\), this is defined whenever:\n\n\\[\n(r,p)\\neq(0,0).\n\\]\n\nThe original formula instead calculates:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\theta_{\\mathrm{old}}\n=\n\\operatorname{atan2}(p,2\\pi r)\n}.\n\\]\n\nThe two satisfy:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\theta_{\\mathrm{old}}+\\theta_4=\\frac{\\pi}{2}\n}.\n\\]\n\nSo the historical expression is not intrinsically meaningless.\n\nIt is the **complementary angle**.\n\nIt becomes incorrect when labeled as the BR-005 time-normal angle.\n\n## 4. Limiting cases\n\nFor a straight filament:\n\n\\[\nr=0,\\qquad p>0,\n\\]\n\nthe correct angle is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\theta_4=0}.\n\\]\n\nThe historical code instead returns:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\theta_{\\mathrm{old}}=90^\\circ}.\n\\]\n\nFor a circular filament with no axial advance:\n\n\\[\nr>0,\\qquad p=0,\n\\]\n\nthe correct angle is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\theta_4=90^\\circ}.\n\\]\n\nThe historical code returns:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\theta_{\\mathrm{old}}=0}.\n\\]\n\nThese are exactly reversed.\n\nAt:\n\n\\[\nr=p=1,\n\\]\n\nthe archived calculation gives:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\theta_{\\mathrm{old}}=9.043061079^\\circ}.\n\\]\n\nThe corrected calculation gives:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\theta_4=80.956938921^\\circ}.\n\\]\n\nThe difference is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{71.913877842^\\circ}.\n\\]\n\nThis is not a rounding discrepancy.\n\nIt is a convention error.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Consequence for the old mass-angle construction\n\nThe historical `SAT-Y Theta4 Calcs.txt` document also explores the constitutive proposal:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{m}{m_{\\max}}=\\sin^2\\theta_4\n}.\n\\]\n\nThis is a historical toy model, not an independently established mass law.\n\nSubstitute the corrected geometry:\n\n\\[\n\\sin^2\\theta_4\n=\n\\frac{r^2}\n{r^2+(p/(2\\pi))^2}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{m}{m_{\\max}}\n=\n\\frac{(2\\pi r)^2}\n{p^2+(2\\pi r)^2}\n}.\n\\]\n\nBut substituting the old complementary angle instead gives:\n\n\\[\n\\sin^2\\theta_{\\mathrm{old}}\n=\n\\cos^2\\theta_4.\n\\]\n\nHence:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\left(\\frac{m}{m_{\\max}}\\right)_{\\mathrm{old}}\n=\n1-\n\\left(\\frac{m}{m_{\\max}}\\right)_{\\mathrm{correct}}\n}.\n\\]\n\n**The angle-convention error reverses the toy mass assignment.**\n\nFor a straight filament:\n\n\\[\nr=0,\n\\]\n\nthe corrected toy model gives:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\frac{m}{m_{\\max}}=0}.\n\\]\n\nThe old implementation gives:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\frac{m}{m_{\\max}}=1}.\n\\]\n\nThat directly contradicts the current straight-vacuum baseline.\n\nThe geometrical correction is established.\n\nThe mass-angle constitutive law is not.\n\nNo particle mass has been predicted from independent inputs here.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Four-dimensional finite-core consequence\n\nThis correction also clarifies a potentially confusing statement in ND-2026-10-18-07.\n\nConsider an infinite straight Euclidean four-dimensional solid worldtube with intrinsic normal radius \\(\\epsilon\\).\n\nLet its unit tangent be:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nT=\n(\\sin\\theta_4,0,0,\\cos\\theta_4)\n}.\n\\]\n\nFor any point \\(X\\), the squared perpendicular distance to its axis is:\n\n\\[\nd_\\perp^2=\n\\|X\\|^2-(X\\cdot T)^2.\n\\]\n\nTake the three-dimensional slice:\n\n\\[\nw=0.\n\\]\n\nThen:\n\n\\[\nX=(x,y,z,0).\n\\]\n\nTherefore:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_\\perp^2=\nx^2\\cos^2\\theta_4+y^2+z^2\n}.\n\\]\n\nThe solid tube intersects the slice wherever:\n\n\\[\nd_\\perp^2\\leq\\epsilon^2.\n\\]\n\nThis is an ellipsoid with semiaxes:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\left(\n\\frac{\\epsilon}{|\\cos\\theta_4|},\n\\epsilon,\n\\epsilon\n\\right)\n}.\n\\]\n\nIts volume is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV=\n\\frac{4\\pi\\epsilon^3}\n{3|\\cos\\theta_4|}\n}.\n\\]\n\nND-2026-10-18-07 records an oblique-slice expression involving:\n\n\\[\n\\frac{\\epsilon}{|\\sin\\theta|}.\n\\]\n\nThese expressions agree when:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\theta=\\theta_{\\mathrm{plane}}\n=\n\\frac{\\pi}{2}-\\theta_4\n}.\n\\]\n\nBecause:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\sin\\theta_{\\mathrm{plane}}\n=\n\\cos\\theta_4\n}.\n\\]\n\n**Thus the two formulas are compatible if their angles are explicitly distinguished.**\n\nThe calculation also establishes their limiting behavior.\n\nAt:\n\n\\[\n\\theta_4=0,\n\\]\n\nthe slice is spherical.\n\nAs:\n\n\\[\n\\theta_4\\rightarrow90^\\circ,\n\\]\n\nthe ideal infinite straight tube's slice becomes unbounded.\n\nThis does not mean an actual finite helical worldtube develops infinite volume.\n\nThe infinite-straight-tube construction has ceased to be an appropriate approximation.\n\nFor a curved helix, the local curvature is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\kappa=\n\\frac{r}\n{r^2+(p/(2\\pi))^2}\n}.\n\\]\n\nThe local straight-core approximation requires:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\epsilon\\kappa\\ll1\n}.\n\\]\n\nThat condition must be checked rather than presumed.\n\n---\n\n# 7. The finite time-slab calculation\n\nConsider an idealized straight, uniform, solid four-dimensional worldtube.\n\nIts intrinsic radius is:\n\n\\[\n\\epsilon.\n\\]\n\nIts unit tangent makes an angle \\(\\theta_4\\) with the time normal:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nT=\n(\\sin\\theta_4,0,0,\\cos\\theta_4)\n}.\n\\]\n\nThe finite active time-wavefront occupies:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n-\\frac d2\\leq w\\leq\\frac d2\n}.\n\\]\n\nHere \\(d\\) is the slab thickness, measured in length units.\n\nFor a point:\n\n\\[\nX=(x,y,z,w),\n\\]\n\nthe squared perpendicular distance to the worldtube axis is:\n\n\\[\nd_\\perp^2\n=\n\\|X\\|^2-(X\\cdot T)^2.\n\\]\n\nExpanding:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_\\perp^2=\n(x\\cos\\theta_4-w\\sin\\theta_4)^2+y^2+z^2\n}.\n\\]\n\nThe solid worldtube consists of points satisfying:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_\\perp^2\\leq\\epsilon^2\n}.\n\\]\n\nThis is the complete geometric constraint for the idealized object.\n\n## A. One instantaneous three-dimensional intersection\n\nAt fixed \\(w\\):\n\n\\[\n(x\\cos\\theta_4-w\\sin\\theta_4)^2+y^2+z^2\n\\leq\\epsilon^2.\n\\]\n\nFor \\(0\\leq\\theta_4<90^\\circ\\), rearranging gives:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\cos^2\\theta_4\n(x-w\\tan\\theta_4)^2+y^2+z^2\n\\leq\\epsilon^2\n}.\n\\]\n\nThis is an ellipsoid centered at:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{x=w\\tan\\theta_4}.\n\\]\n\nIts semiaxes are:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\na=\\frac{\\epsilon}{\\cos\\theta_4},\n\\qquad b=c=\\epsilon\n}.\n\\]\n\nIts volume is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_{\\mathrm{slice}}\n=\n\\frac{4\\pi\\epsilon^3}{3\\cos\\theta_4}\n}.\n\\]\n\nThis agrees with the corresponding oblique-slice construction in ND-2026-10-18-07 when the complementary angle conventions are reconciled.\n\n## B. The complete finite-thickness intersection\n\nNow consider every three-dimensional slice within the slab.\n\nAs \\(w\\) varies, the ellipsoid's center moves along the \\(x\\)-axis.\n\nThe total displacement is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nL=d|\\tan\\theta_4|\n}.\n\\]\n\nThe union of the slices is the original ellipsoid extruded along that interval.\n\nIts volume is the original ellipsoid volume plus the extrusion length multiplied by the transverse area:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_{\\mathrm{support}}\n=\nV_{\\mathrm{slice}}\n+\n\\pi\\epsilon^2L\n}.\n\\]\n\nSubstituting:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_{\\mathrm{support}}\n=\n\\frac{4\\pi\\epsilon^3}{3\\cos\\theta_4}\n+\n\\pi\\epsilon^2d|\\tan\\theta_4|\n}.\n\\]\n\nDivide by the single-slice volume:\n\n\\[\n\\frac{V_{\\mathrm{support}}}{V_{\\mathrm{slice}}}\n=\n1+\n\\frac{\n\\pi\\epsilon^2d|\\tan\\theta_4|\n}{\n4\\pi\\epsilon^3/(3\\cos\\theta_4)\n}.\n\\]\n\nSimplifying:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{V_{\\mathrm{support}}}{V_{\\mathrm{slice}}}\n=\n1+\\frac{3d|\\sin\\theta_4|}{4\\epsilon}\n}.\n\\]\n\nThis is the principal new geometrical result.\n\nThe finite-thickness amplification depends only on the dimensionless ratio \\(d/\\epsilon\\) and the tilt angle.\n\n---\n\n# 5. A second readout gives a different answer\n\nSuppose the three-dimensional observer does not register every location occupied at any moment in the slab.\n\nInstead, define the time-averaged occupancy:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\rho(x,y,z)\n=\n\\frac1d\n\\int_{-d/2}^{d/2}\n\\mathbf1_{\\mathrm{tube}}(x,y,z,w)\\,dw\n}.\n\\]\n\nHere \\(\\mathbf1_{\\mathrm{tube}}\\) is one inside the tube and zero outside.\n\nThe spatial support of \\(\\rho\\) is the union volume just calculated.\n\nHowever, integrating \\(\\rho\\) over three-dimensional space gives:\n\n\\[\n\\int\\rho\\,d^3x\n=\n\\frac1d\n\\int_{-d/2}^{d/2}\n\\left(\n\\int\\mathbf1_{\\mathrm{tube}}\\,d^3x\n\\right)dw.\n\\]\n\nEvery fixed-\\(w\\) intersection has the same volume.\n\nTherefore:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\int\\rho\\,d^3x\n=\nV_{\\mathrm{slice}}\n}.\n\\]\n\nWe now have two different quantities:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_{\\mathrm{support}}\n>\nV_{\\mathrm{slice}}\n}\n\\]\n\nfor nonzero slab thickness and tilt, while:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\int\\rho\\,d^3x=V_{\\mathrm{slice}}\n}.\n\\]\n\n**The support volume grows with slab thickness. The integrated mean occupancy does not.**\n\nThat distinction is mathematical, not interpretive.\n\nIt does not establish which quantity corresponds to observed particle volume, inertia, mass, or electromagnetic response.\n\nThose require a specified physical readout.\n\n---\n\n# 6.   (R+u)*sp.sin(ph)-z*A*sp.cos(ph)/B,\n    v,\n    A*ph+z*R/B\n])\n\nJ=sp.simplify(\n    X.jacobian([ph,u,v,z]).det()\n)\n\nexpected=B+R*u/B\n\nassert sp.simplify(\n    sp.trigsimp(sp.expand(J))+expected\n)==0\n\nprint('SYMBOLIC oriented_J=-(b+(r/b)*u); '\n      'absolute_J=b+(r/b)*u')\nprint('SYMBOLIC J=b+(r/b)*u PASS')\n\n# Slab volume.\neps=0.2\nd=0.8\n\nVball=4*math.pi*eps**3/3\nV3=b/a*Vball\nV4=d*V3\n\nprint('VOLUME eps=%.6f d=%.6f V_ball=%.12f '\n      'V_slice_exact=%.12f V4_slab=%.12f'%\n      (eps,d,Vball,V3,V4))\n\n# Numerical Jacobian test.\ndef mapX(t,q):\n    U,V,Z=q\n    return np.array([\n        (r+U)*math.cos(t)+Z*a*math.sin(t)/b,\n        (r+U)*math.sin(t)-Z*a*math.cos(t)/b,\n        V,\n        a*t+Z*r/b\n    ])\n\nrng=np.random.default_rng(20261018)\n\nmaxerr=0\n\nfor _ in range(40):\n    t=rng.uniform(-4,4)\n    q=rng.uniform(-eps,eps,3)\n\n    step=1e-5\n    xx=np.array([t,*q])\n    derivs=[]\n\n    for j in range(4):\n        xp=xx.copy()\n        xm=xx.copy()\n\n        xp[j]+=step\n        xm[j]-=step\n\n        derivs.append(\n            (mapX(xp[0],xp[1:])\n             -mapX(xm[0],xm[1:]))/(2*step)\n        )\n\n    num=abs(\n        np.linalg.det(\n            np.column_stack(derivs)\n        )\n    )\n\n    exact=b+r*q[0]/b\n    maxerr=max(maxerr,abs(num-exact))\n\nassert maxerr<1e-8\n\nprint('NUMERICAL_JACOBIAN max_abs_error=%.3e PASS'%maxerr)\n\n# Independent Monte Carlo integration.\nN=250000\n\nunit=rng.normal(size=(N,3))\nunit/=np.linalg.norm(unit,axis=1)[:,None]\n\nq=unit*(rng.random(N)**(1/3)*eps)[:,None]\n\nmcV3=Vball*np.mean(\n    (b+r*q[:,0]/b)/a\n)\n\nrelative=mcV3/V3-1\n\nassert abs(relative)<0.005\n\nprint('MC_VOLUME samples=%d estimate=%.12f '\n      'exact=%.12f rel_error=%+.8f PASS'%\n      (N,mcV3,V3,relative))\n\n# exactx=(r+U)*np.cos(PH)+Z*a*np.sin(PH)/b\n    exacty=(r+U)*np.sin(PH)-Z*a*np.cos(PH)/b\n\n    approxx=r+U\n    approxy=-b*Z/a\n\n    return exactx,exacty,approxx,approxy\n\nerrors=[]\n\nfor e in      (errors[1]/errors[0]))\n\n# Curvature and torsion.\nkappa=r/b**2\ntau=a/b**2\n\nprint('CURVATURE kappa=%.12f torsion=%.12f '\n      'tau_over_kappa=%.12f'%\n      (kappa,tau,tau/kappa))\n\nassert math.isclose(\n    tau/kappa,\n    p/(2*math.pi*r)\n)\n\n# Limiting and dimensional scaling controls.\nfor scale in [1e-4,1e-2,1,1e2]:\n    rr=r*scale\n    aa=a*scale\n    ee=eps*scale\n    dd=d*scale\n\n    vv=(\n        math.hypot(rr,aa)/aa\n    )*(4*math.pi*ee**3/3)\n\n    assert math.isclose(\n        vv/V3,\n        scale**3,\n        rel_tol=1e-12\n    )\n\nassert math.isclose(\n    (math.hypot(0,a)/a)*Vball,\n    Vball\n)\n\nprint('LIMITS r_to_zero_straight_tube=PASS '\n      'common_length_scaling_cubic=PASS')\n\n# Class P New result: exact finite-core intersection centroid\n\nKestrel derived the instantaneous intersection volume of a solid four-dimensional helical tube.\n\nI extended that calculation to determine **where the center of the intersection actually lies**.\n\nThis is not automatically the same as the centerline position.\n\n## The four-dimensional helix\n\nUse length coordinates:\n\n\\[\nC(\\phi)=\n(r\\cos\\phi,r\\sin\\phi,0,a\\phi),\n\\]\n\nwhere:\n\n\\[\na=\\frac{p}{2\\pi},\n\\qquad\nb=\\sqrt{r^2+a^2}.\n\\]\n\nIts unit tangent is:\n\n\\[\nT(\\phi)=\n\\frac1b\n(-r\\sin\\phi,r\\cos\\phi,0,a).\n\\]\n\nIntroduce the normal frame:\n\n\\[\nN_1=(\\cos\\phi,\\sin\\phi,0,0),\n\\]\n\n\\[\nN_2=(0,0,1,0),\n\\]\n\n\\[\nN_3=\n\\frac1b\n(a\\sin\\phi,-a\\cos\\phi,0,r).\n\\]\n\nThe finite-core tube is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nX=C+uN_1+vN_2+zN_3\n}\n\\]\n\nwith:\n\n\\[\nu^2+v^2+z^2\\leq\\epsilon^2.\n\\]\n\nHere \\(\\epsilon\\) is intrinsic core thickness.\n\nIt is not the coil radius \\(r\\).\n\n## The intersection Jacobian\n\nThe absolute four-dimensional Jacobian is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nJ=b+\\frac rb u\n}\n\\]\n\nfor a regular embedded tube.\n\nThe time coordinate is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nw=a\\phi+\\frac rb z.\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore, at fixed \\(w\\):\n\n\\[\n\\phi=\\frac wa-\\frac{r}{ab}z.\n\\]\n\nDefine:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nk=\\frac{r}{ab}\n}\n\\]\n\nand:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nq=k\\epsilon.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe instantaneous three-dimensional intersection volume is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_3=\n\\frac ba\\frac{4\\pi\\epsilon^3}{3}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThat reproduces Kestrel's result.\n\nNow calculate the centroid.\n\n---\n\n# 5. The exact centroid formula\n\nAt \\(w=0\\), the first spatial coordinate is:\n\n\\[\nx=\n(r+u)\\cos(kz)\n-\n\\frac ab z\\sin(kz).\n\\]\n\nWe must integrate this over the normal ball using the correct Jacobian.\n\nIntroduce:\n\n\\[\nF(q)=\n\\frac1{V_B}\n\\int_{B_\\epsilon}\\cos(kz)\\,d^3n.\n\\]\n\nDirect integration gives:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nF(q)=\n\\frac{3(\\sin q-q\\cos q)}{q^3}\n}\n\\]\n\nwith:\n\n\\[\nF(0)=1.\n\\]\n\nRotational symmetry of the normal ball gives two useful identities:\n\n\\[\n\\left\\langle\nu^2\\cos(kz)\n\\right\\rangle\n=\n-\\frac{F'(k)}{k},\n\\]\n\nand:\n\n\\[\n\\left\\langle\nz\\sin(kz)\n\\right\\rangle\n=\n-F'(k).\n\\]\n\nThe weighted centroid becomes:\n\n\\[\n\\bar x\n=\nrF(k)\n-\n\\frac{r}{b^2k}F'(k)\n+\n\\frac abF'(k).\n\\]\n\nBut:\n\n\\[\n\\frac{r}{b^2k}\n=\n\\frac ab.\n\\]\n\nTherefore the final two terms cancel exactly.\n\nWe obtain:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\bar x=rF(q).\n}\n\\]\n\nBy symmetry:\n\n\\[\n\\bar y=\\bar z=0\n\\]\n\nat \\(w=0\\).\n\nThe helix has screw-translation symmetry, so the centroid rotates with the time coordinate.\n\nThe complete result is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\displaystyle\nM(w)=\nrF(q)\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n\\cos(w/a)\\\\\n\\sin(w/a)\\\\\n0\n\\end{pmatrix}\n}\n\\]\n\nwhere:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nq=\\frac{r\\epsilon}{a\\sqrt{r^2+a^2}}.\n}\n\\]\n\n**This is an exact geometrical result for the specified regular, embedded, uniform solid tube.**\n\nIt is not a particle-mass formula or a dynamical force law.\n\n---\n\n# 6. The small-core limit\n\nExpand the function:\n\n\\[\nF(q)=\n1-\\frac{q^2}{10}\n+\\frac{q^4}{280}\n+O(q^6).\n\\]\n\nTherefore:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nr-M_x(0)\n=\n\\frac{rq^2}{10}\n+O(q^4).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe displacement is quadratic in intrinsic core thickness at leading order.\n\nConsequently, the centerline approximation becomes increasingly accurate as:\n\n\\[\n\\epsilon\\rightarrow0.\n\\]\n\nBut it is not exact at finite thickness.\n\nThis supplies a quantitative approximation error rather than merely declaring the centerline an approximation.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Finite time-slab averaging\n\nElias Kern previously distinguished the support union from mean occupancy across a finite time-wavefront slab.\n\nWe can now derive the centroid of that mean occupancy for the actual helix.\n\nDefine:\n\n\\[\n\\rho_d(x,y,z)\n=\n\\frac1d\n\\int_{-d/2}^{d/2}\n\\mathbf1_{\\mathrm{tube}}(x,y,z,w)\\,dw.\n\\]\n\nEvery instantaneous slice has equal volume.\n\nTherefore the centroid of mean occupancy is the average of the instantaneous centroids:\n\n\\[\n\\bar M_d\n=\n\\frac1d\n\\int_{-d/2}^{d/2}\nM(w)\\,dw.\n\\]\n\nSubstituting the helical centroid:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\displaystyle\n\\bar M_d=\nrF(q)\n\\operatorname{sinc}\\left(\\frac{\\pi d}{p}\\right)\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n1\\\\0\\\\0\n\\end{pmatrix}\n}\n\\]\n\nwhere:\n\n\\[\n\\operatorname{sinc}(x)=\\frac{\\sin x}{x}.\n\\]\n\nAt:\n\n\\[\nd=p,\n\\]\n\nthe mean-occupancy centroid is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\bar M_p=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe same occurs at any positive integer multiple of the pitch.\n\nThis follows from averaging over complete helical revolutions.\n\n**It does not mean the particle vanishes or that its interactions cancel.**\n\nIt means this particular first-moment readout loses the information about the instantaneous centroid's angular position.\n\nThat distinction is important for coarse-graining.\n\n![Finite-slab centroid averaging](sandbox:/mnt/data/sable_20261018_22z_slab_centroid.png)\n\n---\n\n# 9.
