Reconstructing the optical calculation\n\nThe historical angular profile can be simplified to:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\theta_4(x)=\n\\frac{\\pi}{3}\n\\left[1+\\tanh(\\mu x)\\right].\n}\n\\]\n\nFor this calculation, define:\n\n\\[\n\\mu>0\n\\]\n\nas an inverse wall-width parameter.\n\nIts units are:\n\n\\[\n[\\mu]=\\mathrm{m}^{-1}.\n\\]\n\nThe refractive modulation is:\n\n\\[\n\\Delta n(x)=\n\\eta\\sin^2\n\\left[\n\\frac{\\pi}{3}\n\\left(1+\\tanh(\\mu x)\\right)\n\\right].\n\\]\n\nHere \\(\\eta\\) is dimensionless.\n\nUnder a scalar, reflection-free optical phase approximation:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta\\phi=\n\\frac{2\\pi}{\\lambda}\n\\int\\Delta n(x)\\,dx\n}\n\\]\n\nwhere \\(\\lambda\\) is the vacuum wavelength.\n\nThis phase formula is a separate optical approximation, not a derived SAT dynamical law.\n\nIt assumes that scalar index accumulation is the relevant readout. It does not model reflections, polarization mixing, or noncommuting Jones matrices.\n\n---\n\n# 5. The asymptotic failure\n\nEvaluate the angular profile at both ends.\n\nAs:\n\n\\[\nx\\rightarrow-\\infty,\n\\]\n\nwe have:\n\n\\[\n\\tanh(\\mu x)\\rightarrow-1.\n\\]\n\nTherefore:\n\n\\[\n\\theta_4(-\\infty)=0.\n\\]\n\nConsequently:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta n(-\\infty)=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nNow consider:\n\n\\[\nx\\rightarrow+\\infty.\n\\]\n\nThen:\n\n\\[\n\\tanh(\\mu x)\\rightarrow1.\n\\]\n\nTherefore:\n\n\\[\n\\theta_4(+\\infty)=\\frac{2\\pi}{3}.\n\\]\n\nThe refractive modulation becomes:\n\n\\[\n\\Delta n(+\\infty)\n=\n\\eta\\sin^2\\left(\\frac{2\\pi}{3}\\right).\n\\]\n\nSince:\n\n\\[\n\\sin^2\\left(\\frac{2\\pi}{3}\\right)=\\frac34,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta n(+\\infty)=\\frac34\\eta.\n}\n\\]\n\n**The two asymptotes differ.**\n\nThe index modulation is not localized around the wall.\n\nIt is a transition between two different refractive-index baselines.\n\nThat does not invalidate the domain-wall geometry itself. It invalidates the particular description of its optical modulation as a localized bump.\n\n## Class P: actual refractive profile\n\n![Historical SAT optical kink and reference step](sandbox:/mnt/data/mira_20261018_23z_kink_profile.png)\n\nThe solid curve is the archived refractive-index modulation.\n\nThe dashed curve is a sharp step connecting its asymptotic values.\n\nTheir difference has a finite signed integral.\n\nThe original refractive-index modulation does not.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Why the original phase integral is incomplete\n\nConsider a symmetric observation interval:\n\n\\[\n-L\\leq x\\leq L.\n\\]\n\nThe accumulated phase is:\n\n\\[\n\\Delta\\phi_L=\n\\frac{2\\pi\\eta}{\\lambda}\n\\int_{-L}^{L}\n\\sin^2\\theta_4(x)\\,dx.\n\\]\n\nIntroduce the dimensionless coordinate:\n\n\\[\nu=\\mu x.\n\\]\n\nThen:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta\\phi_L=\n\\frac{2\\pi\\eta}{\\lambda\\mu}\n\\int_{-\\mu L}^{\\mu L}\n\\sin^2\n\\left[\n\\frac{\\pi}{3}(1+\\tanh u)\n\\right]du.\n}\n\\]\n\nDefine:\n\n\\[\nU=\\mu L.\n\\]\n\nFor large \\(U\\), the integral grows as:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nI(U)=\\frac34U+C+o(1).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe constant \\(C\\) is finite.\n\nBut the first term increases linearly with the observation window.\n\nTherefore:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\lim_{L\\rightarrow\\infty}\\Delta\\phi_L\n}\n\\]\n\ndoes not exist as a finite number for nonzero \\(\\eta\\).\n\n**The historical 0.125-radian result cannot be uniquely reconstructed from the archived equations alone.**\n\nA finite optical path or a specified reference phase is required.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Recovering a finite phase functional\n\nThe natural mathematical repair is to define a reference consisting of the two asymptotic refractive media joined by an abrupt step.\n\nLet:\n\n\\[\n\\Delta n_{\\mathrm{step}}(x)=\n\\begin{cases}\n0,&x<0,\\\\[4pt]\n\\frac34\\eta,&x>0.\n\\end{cases}\n\\]\n\nThen define the excess phase:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta\\phi_{\\mathrm{excess}}\n=\n\\frac{2\\pi}{\\lambda}\n\\int_{-\\infty}^{\\infty}\n\\left[\n\\Delta n(x)-\n\\Delta n_{\\mathrm{step}}(x)\n\\right]dx.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis integral converges.\n\nSubstituting the archived profile gives:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta\\phi_{\\mathrm{excess}}\n=\n\\frac{2\\pi\\eta}{\\lambda\\mu}C\n}\n\\]\n\nwhere:\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\nC={}&\n\\int_{-\\infty}^{0}\n\\sin^2\n\\left[\n\\frac{\\pi}{3}(1+\\tanh u)\n\\right]du\\\\\n&+\n\\int_0^\\infty\n\\left\\{\n\\sin^2\n\\left[\n\\frac{\\pi}{3}(1+\\tanh u)\n\\right]\n-\\frac34\n\\right\\}du.\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nThis is a finite, dimensionless geometrical-optical quantity.\n\n### An independent symmetry reduction\n\nThe two halves can be combined.\n\nUsing:\n\n\\[\n\\sin^2 A+\\sin^2 B\n=\n1-\\cos(A+B)\\cos(A-B),\n\\]\n\nwith:\n\n\\[\nA=\\frac{\\pi}{3}(1+\\tanh u)\n\\]\n\nand:\n\n\\[\nB=\\frac{\\pi}{3}(1-\\tanh u),\n\\]\n\nwe obtain:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nC=\n\\int_0^\\infty\n\\left[\n\\frac14+\n\\frac12\\cos\n\\left(\n\\frac{2\\pi}{3}\\tanh u\n\\right)\n\\right]du.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis expression is independently integrable.\n\nThe executed calculation gives:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nC=0.644705110353796.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe finite excess-phase formula is therefore:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\displaystyle\n\\Delta\\phi_{\\mathrm{excess}}\n=\n0.644705110353796\n\\frac{2\\pi\\eta}{\\lambda\\mu}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is the principal corrected mathematical result.\n\nIt does not prove that the step-referenced observable is what the original simulation measured.\n\nThat identification remains unresolved.\n\n---\n\n# 8. Additional result: overlapping gates are not always independent\n\nAfter preparing the initial publication checkpoint, I extended the calculation to overlapping triplet constraints.\n\nThis revealed a useful general theorem.\n\nRepresent a collection of \\(\\mathbb Z_3\\) constraints as a matrix:\n\n\\[\nAq=0\\pmod3.\n\\]\n\nFor independent uniform site labels:\n\n\\[\nq\\in\\mathbb F_3^n,\n\\]\n\nthe number of solutions is:\n\n\\[\n3^{n-\\operatorname{rank}(A)}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(Aq=0)=\n3^{-\\operatorname{rank}_{\\mathbb F_3}(A)}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis gives the exact joint null probability for any specified collection of linear fusion constraints.\n\n### A four-site counterexample\n\nConsider four sites and four overlapping triplets.\n\nEach triplet contains three of the four sites.\n\nThe incidence matrix is:\n\n\\[\nA=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n0&1&1&1\\\\\n1&0&1&1\\\\\n1&1&0&1\\\\\n1&1&1&0\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nOver \\(\\mathbb F_3\\), the sum of the four rows is zero.\n\nThe matrix therefore has rank three, not four.\n\nThe probability that all four constraints hold is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP=\\frac1{27}.\n}\n\\]\n\nIf the four gates were independent, the answer would instead be:\n\n\\[\n\\frac1{81}.\n\\]\n\nExhaustive enumeration confirms the actual result:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n3\\text{ satisfying assignments out of }81.\n}\n\\]\n\nAny three of the four gates are independent, but all four together are not.\n\n**This means overlapping lattice constraints can possess higher-order dependencies even when individual and pairwise statistics appear ordinary.**\n\nIt is a useful warning for interpreting the historical two-dimensional fusion simulations.\n\n---\n\n# 9. A bounded geometrical calculation\n\nTo isolate the mathematical behavior of the recovered timewave term, consider a circular helix embedded in four-dimensional Euclidean coordinates:\n\n\\[\nX(\\phi)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\nr\\cos\\phi\\\\\nr\\sin\\phi\\\\\n0\\\\\nH\\phi/(2\\pi N)\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nHere:\n\n\\[\n0\\leq\\phi\\leq2\\pi N.\n\\]\n\nThe parameters are:\n\n- \\(r>0\\), helix radius.\n- \\(H>0\\), total longitudinal advance.\n- \\(N\\geq1\\), integer winding number.\n- \\(\\alpha>0\\), constant timewave coefficient.\n\nThese are explicit test assumptions, not claims that the complete historical SAT action uses this particular parameterization.\n\nThe total arclength is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nL=\\sqrt{H^2+(2\\pi Nr)^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nSet the timewave direction to:\n\n\\[\n\\hat T=e_w.\n\\]\n\nFor this bounded test, choose the integration parameter to be Euclidean arclength \\(s\\).\n\nThen:\n\n\\[\n\\frac{dX}{ds}\\cdot e_w=\\frac HL.\n\\]\n\nThe timewave action becomes:\n\n\\[\nS_{\\mathrm{tw}}\n=\n\\alpha\n\\int_0^L\n\\left(\n\\frac{dX}{ds}\\cdot e_w\n\\right)^2ds.\n\\]\n\nSubstitution gives:\n\n\\[\nS_{\\mathrm{tw}}\n=\n\\alpha\\int_0^L\\frac{H^2}{L^2}\\,ds.\n\\]\n\nTherefore:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nS_{\\mathrm{tw}}=\\frac{\\alpha H^2}{L}.\n}\n\\]\n\nOr:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nS_{\\mathrm{tw}}(r)\n=\n\\frac{\\alpha H^2}\n{\\sqrt{H^2+(2\\pi Nr)^2}}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis expression was checked symbolically and by independent numerical quadrature.\n\n---\n\n# 4. Does topology determine the action?\n\nDifferentiate with respect to radius:\n\n\\[\n\\frac{dS_{\\mathrm{tw}}}{dr}\n=\n-\\frac{\n\\alpha H^2(2\\pi N)^2r\n}{\n[H^2+(2\\pi Nr)^2]^{3/2}\n}.\n\\]\n\nFor positive \\(r,H,\\alpha\\):\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{dS_{\\mathrm{tw}}}{dr}<0.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe action decreases continuously as the helix radius increases.\n\nAt fixed winding number and longitudinal advance, the restricted functional has no finite interior minimum.\n\nIts infimum is zero as:\n\n\\[\nr\\rightarrow\\infty.\n\\]\n\nThis does not demonstrate that the full SAT action lacks a stable extremum. Additional bending, interaction, core, or boundary terms could select one.\n\nIt establishes that the displayed timewave term alone does not do so.\n\n## Three strands versus one\n\nNow construct three phase-separated helices.\n\nTheir phases are:\n\n\\[\n0,\\qquad\\frac{2\\pi}{3},\\qquad\\frac{4\\pi}{3}.\n\\]\n\nAt positive radius, the strands remain nonintersecting.\n\nWith identical coefficients and longitudinal advances, their total timewave action is:\n\n\\[\nS_3=\n\\frac{3\\alpha H^2}{L_h}.\n\\]\n\nFor a single electron-solenoid test curve:\n\n\\[\nS_1=\n\\frac{\\alpha H^2}{L_e}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{S_3}{S_1}\n=\n3\\frac{L_e}{L_h}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is not generally equal to three, much less:\n\n\\[\n\\frac{3}{2B^5}.\n\\]\n\n### Executed numerical test\n\nFix:\n\n\\[\nH=N=\\alpha=1,\n\\qquad\nr_e=0.1.\n\\]\n\nThen vary the three-strand radius.\n\n| Three-strand radius | Calculated action ratio |\n|---:|---:|\n| 0.05 | 3.380150053407 |\n| 0.10 | 3.000000000000 |\n| 0.20 | 2.206162912840 |\n| 0.40 | 1.309850356367 |\n| 0.80 | 0.691315417345 |\n\nThe strand arrangement retains its winding and nonintersection structure.\n\nThe action ratio changes substantially.\n\n### Class P: calculated action ratio\n\n![Calculated SAT timewave action ratio under radial variation](sandbox:/mnt/data/enheduanna_20261019_04z_action_ratio.png)\n\nThis is an exact plot of the derived expression, not an illustrative rendering.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Stronger test: preserve the endpoints\n\nUniform radial rescaling changes the positions of the strand endpoints.\n\nTo eliminate that possible objection, I constructed a second family in which **the endpoints remain fixed**.\n\nLet:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nr(\\phi)\n=\nr_0\n\\left[\n1+\\epsilon\\sin^2\\left(\\frac{\\phi}{2}\\right)\n\\right].\n}\n\\]\n\nFor one complete revolution:\n\n\\[\n0\\leq\\phi\\leq2\\pi.\n\\]\n\nAt both endpoints:\n\n\\[\nr(0)=r(2\\pi)=r_0.\n\\]\n\nFor \\(\\epsilon\\geq0\\), the radius remains positive.\n\nThe three strands retain their phase separation and undergo a continuous deformation without crossing.\n\nTheir endpoints and braid isotopy class remain fixed.\n\nThe arclength-gauge action is now:\n\n\\[\nS_{\\mathrm{tw}}\n=\n\\alpha\n\\int_0^{2\\pi}\n\\frac{a^2}\n{\\sqrt{r'(\\phi)^2+r(\\phi)^2+a^2}}\n\\,d\\phi,\n\\]\n\nwhere:\n\n\\[\na=\\frac{H}{2\\pi}.\n\\]\n\nSet:\n\n\\[\nr_0=0.2,\n\\qquad H=\\alpha=1.\n\\]\n\n### Executed results\n\n| Interior deformation \\(\\epsilon\\) | Timewave action |\n|---:|---:|\n| 0.0 | 0.622676992299 |\n| 0.2 | 0.586107360935 |\n| 0.5 | 0.537487389271 |\n| 1.0 | 0.471768341998 |\n\nThe endpoints are unchanged.\n\nThe braid topology is unchanged.\n\nThe timewave action changes.\n\nI also calculated the first derivative analytically:\n\n\\[\n\\left.\n\\frac{dS}{d\\epsilon}\n\\right|_{\\epsilon=0}\n=\n-\\frac{\n\\alpha a^2r_0^2\\pi\n}{\n(r_0^2+a^2)^{3/2}\n}.\n\\]\n\nNumerically:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n-0.190624268150.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe independently evaluated forward difference gives:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n-0.190620668824.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe agreement is within the declared finite-difference tolerance.\n\n**This is the strongest result of the turn.**\n\nThe recovered timewave term does not assign one action value to a braid isotopy class, even with fixed strand endpoints.\n\nA physical extremization must therefore incorporate additional admissibility constraints or action terms.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Correcting the Green function\n\nFor a radially symmetric function in four-dimensional Euclidean space:\n\n\\[\n\\Delta_4f=\nf''(r)+\\frac3r f'(r).\n\\]\n\nTake:\n\n\\[\nf(r)=\\frac A{r^2}.\n\\]\n\nThen:\n\n\\[\nf'(r)=-\\frac{2A}{r^3}\n\\]\n\nand:\n\n\\[\nf''(r)=\\frac{6A}{r^4}.\n\\]\n\nSubstituting:\n\n\\[\n\\Delta_4f=\n\\frac{6A}{r^4}\n-\n\\frac3r\\frac{2A}{r^3}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta_4f=0,\\qquad r>0.\n}\n\\]\n\nBoth signs satisfy the homogeneous equation away from the origin.\n\nThe distinction appears at the singularity.\n\n## Distributional normalization\n\nThe surface area of a three-sphere of radius \\(r\\) is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nA(S_r^3)=2\\pi^2r^3.\n}\n\\]\n\nBy the divergence theorem, the integrated source strength is:\n\n\\[\n\\int_{B_r^4}\\Delta_4f\\,dV\n=\n\\oint_{S_r^3}\\nabla f\\cdot n\\,d\\Sigma.\n\\]\n\nFor the radial function:\n\n\\[\n\\oint_{S_r^3}\\nabla f\\cdot n\\,d\\Sigma\n=\n2\\pi^2r^3f'(r).\n\\]\n\nSubstitute:\n\n\\[\n=\n2\\pi^2r^3\n\\left(\n-\\frac{2A}{r^3}\n\\right).\n\\]\n\nThus:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{Flux}=-4\\pi^2A.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe historical coefficient is:\n\n\\[\nA_{\\mathrm{historical}}=\n+\\frac1{4\\pi^2}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{Flux}_{\\mathrm{historical}}=-1.\n}\n\\]\n\nIt satisfies:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta_4G_{\\mathrm{historical}}\n=\n-\\delta^{(4)}.\n}\n\\]\n\nBut the source explicitly requires a positive delta function.\n\nThe corrected coefficient is:\n\n\\[\nA_{\\mathrm{corrected}}=\n-\\frac1{4\\pi^2}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG_{\\mathrm{corrected}}(r)=\n-\\frac1{4\\pi^2r^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nAnd:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta_4G_{\\mathrm{corrected}}\n=\n+\\delta^{(4)}.\n}\n\\]\n\n### Correction status\n\nThis is uniquely correctable under the source's explicit positive-Laplacian convention and the free-space decay condition.\n\nThe positive Green function would instead be correct for the alternative operator:\n\n\\[\n-\\Delta_4.\n\\]\n\nThe two sign conventions are standard. The historical error is combining one operator convention with the fundamental solution belonging to the other.\n\n**Gate: `CONFIDENTLY CORRECTED / INTERNALLY CHECKED`.**\n\n---\n\n# 4. The more consequential result: timesheet geometry\n\nThe historical document proposes obtaining the galactic-memory kernel through:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal K=\n\\oint_{\\Sigma_w}G_{\\mathrm{top}}\\,d\\sigma.\n}\n\\]\n\nIt claims this uniquely determines the response of historical tethers.\n\nBut the expression depends on the geometry and extent of \\(\\Sigma_w\\).\n\nTo test this, I constructed two explicit geometries using the same corrected four-dimensional Green function.\n\nNeither geometry is asserted to be the final physical SAT timesheet.\n\nThey are controlled mathematical alternatives.\n\n## Case A: Closed three-sphere\n\nLet:\n\n\\[\n\\Sigma_w=S_R^3\n\\]\n\nbe a three-sphere of radius \\(R\\) in Euclidean four-space.\n\nEvaluate the Green function at a point whose distance from the sphere's center is \\(a\\).\n\nThe squared separation from a surface point is:\n\n\\[\n|X-X'|^2=\na^2+R^2-2aR\\cos\\theta.\n\\]\n\nAfter integrating the two angular coordinates, the surface measure becomes:\n\n\\[\nd\\Sigma=\n4\\pi R^3\\sin^2\\theta\\,d\\theta.\n\\]\n\nTherefore:\n\n\\[\n\\mathcal K_R(a)=\n-\\frac{R^3}{\\pi}\n\\int_0^\\pi\n\\frac{\\sin^2\\theta}\n{a^2+R^2-2aR\\cos\\theta}\n\\,d\\theta.\n\\]\n\nThis integral has an exact solution:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal K_R(a)=\n\\begin{cases}\n-\\dfrac R2,&0\\leq a\\leq R,\\\\[6pt]\n-\\dfrac{R^3}{2a^2},&a\\geq R.\n\\end{cases}\n}\n\\]\n\nThe kernel is constant inside the shell.\n\nOutside, it decreases in magnitude as:\n\n\\[\na^{-2}.\n\\]\n\nAt the boundary, the function is continuous, but its radial derivative jumps.\n\nSpecifically:\n\n\\[\n\\left.\n\\frac{d\\mathcal K}{da}\n\\right|_{R^-}=0\n\\]\n\nand:\n\n\\[\n\\left.\n\\frac{d\\mathcal K}{da}\n\\right|_{R^+}=1.\n\\]\n\nTherefore:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\left[\n\\frac{d\\mathcal K}{da}\n\\right]_{R^-}^{R^+}=1.\n}\n\\]\n\nThat is exactly the derivative jump expected for unit surface source density.\n\n### Class P visualization\n\n![Exact integrated 4D Green function over a three-sphere](sandbox:/mnt/data/aster_20261019_06z_shell_kernel.png)\n\nThe numerical quadrature reproduced the exact result at 24 combinations of shell radius and evaluation position.\n\n**All 24 comparisons passed.**\n\nThis is an internally checked mathematical shell construction.\n\nIt is not yet a physical model of gravitational memory.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Case B: Noncompact flat timesheet\n\nNow use a three-dimensional hyperplane in the same four-dimensional Euclidean space.\n\nLet \\(a\\) be the perpendicular distance from the evaluation point to the plane.\n\nTruncate the plane at radius \\(L\\).\n\nThe integral becomes:\n\n\\[\n\\mathcal K_L(a)=\n-\\frac1{4\\pi^2}\n\\int_{|\\mathbf y|\\leq L}\n\\frac{d^3y}{|\\mathbf y|^2+a^2}.\n\\]\n\nIn Test A: Does a three-strand braid have Hausdorff dimension four?\n\nConsider three smooth worldlines embedded in Euclidean four-space.\n\nDefine:\n\n\\[\n\\gamma_j(t)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n\\cos(t+\\phi_j)\\\\\n\\sin(t+\\phi_j)\\\\\n0.15\\sin(2t+\\phi_j)\\\\\nt\n\\end{pmatrix}\n\\]\n\nwith:\n\n\\[\n0\\leq t\\leq2\\pi\n\\]\n\nand:\n\n\\[\n\\phi_j=\\frac{2\\pi j}{3},\n\\qquad j=0,1,2.\n\\]\n\nThese are explicit four-dimensional curves.\n\nEach curve is continuously differentiable, with bounded derivative on the specified interval.\n\nTherefore, each is a Lipschitz image of a one-dimensional interval.\n\nConsequently:\n\n\\[\n\\dim_H(\\gamma_j)\\leq1.\n\\]\n\nBut projection onto the fourth coordinate gives:\n\n\\[\n\\pi_w(\\gamma_j(t))=t.\n\\]\n\nIts image contains the entire interval:\n\n\\[\n[0,2\\pi].\n\\]\n\nSince Lipschitz maps cannot increase Hausdorff dimension:\n\n\\[\n\\dim_H(\\gamma_j)\\geq1.\n\\]\n\nCombining both inequalities:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\dim_H(\\gamma_j)=1.\n}\n\\]\n\nA finite union has Hausdorff dimension equal to the maximum dimension of its members.\n\nTherefore:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\dim_H\\left(\n\\bigcup_{j=0}^{2}\\gamma_j\n\\right)=1.\n}\n\\]\n\n**Three smooth one-dimensional worldlines do not acquire Hausdorff dimension four merely by occupying a four-dimensional ambient space.**\n\n### Numerical test\n\nI generated 270,000 sampled points across the three curves and performed four-dimensional box counting.\n\n| Box width \\(\\epsilon\\) | Occupied boxes |\n|---:|---:|\n| 0.500000 | 76 |\n| 0.250000 | 163 |\n| 0.125000 | 358 |\n| 0.062500 | 722 |\n| 0.031250 | 1,454 |\n| 0.015625 | 2,938 |\n\nA log-log regression gave:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_{\\mathrm{box,finite}}\\approx1.052764.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe finite-resolution result is consistent with one-dimensional scaling.\n\nIt is not itself a proof of Hausdorff dimension. The Lipschitz and projection arguments provide that proof for this explicit fixture.\n\n### Class P: Four-dimensional box counting\n\n![Three embedded smooth worldlines retain one-dimensional box-count scaling](sandbox:/mnt/data/calder_20261019_07z_boxcount.png)\n\n### Finite-core distinction\n\nThis finding does not settle the dimension of an H(s)H worldtube.\n\nA smooth one-dimensional centerline has Hausdorff dimension one.\n\nA smooth ribbon can have dimension two.\n\nA smooth boundary of a four-dimensional solid tube can have dimension three.\n\nA solid four-dimensional tube with nonempty interior has dimension four.\n\nThose are different geometric objects.\n\nThe historical argument substitutes the ambient dimension for the centerline's Hausdorff dimension without deriving that substitution.\n\n**The exponent \\(p=3\\) is therefore not established by the historical Hausdorff argument.**\n\n---\n\n# 4. Test B: Does inverse-cubic tension produce divergent separation work?\n\nTake the historical tension law:\n\n\\[\n\\mathcal T(r)=\nk\\frac{Lk\\cdot Wr}{r^3}.\n\\]\n\nFor this bounded test, hold the coefficient fixed:\n\n\\[\nK=kLkWr.\n\\]\n\nThen:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal T(r)=\\frac K{r^3}.\n}\n\\]\n\nConsider a radial separation path from \\(R>0\\) to \\(L>R\\).\n\nThe work is:\n\n\\[\nW(R,L)=\n\\int_R^L\\frac K{r^3}\\,dr.\n\\]\n\nIntegrating:\n\n\\[\nW(R,L)=\nK\\left[-\\frac1{2r^2}\\right]_R^L.\n\\]\n\nTherefore:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nW(R,L)=\n\\frac K2\n\\left(\n\\frac1{R^2}-\\frac1{L^2}\n\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nNow take:\n\n\\[\nL\\rightarrow\\infty.\n\\]\n\nSince:\n\n\\[\n\\frac1{L^2}\\rightarrow0,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\lim_{L\\rightarrow\\infty}\nW(R,L)=\n\\frac K{2R^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\n**The work is finite.**\n\nThe claimed divergence occurs in the opposite limit:\n\n\\[\nR\\rightarrow0^+.\n\\]\n\nThus the historical inverse-cubic expression has a short-distance singularity, not an infinite-separation energy barrier.\n\n### Independent numerical replication\n\nUsing:\n\n\\[\nK=1,\\qquad R=1,\n\\]\n\nthe executed SciPy quadrature produced:\n\n| Final separation \\(L\\) | Work |\n|---:|---:|\n| 2 | 0.375000000000 |\n| 4 | 0.468750000000 |\n| 10 | 0.495000000000 |\n| 100 | 0.499950000000 |\n| 1,000 | 0.499999500000 |\n| \\(\\infty\\) | 0.500000000000 |\n\nAll numerical comparisons passed.\n\n### Class P: Work saturation\n\n![Inverse-cubic tension produces finite separation work](sandbox:/mnt/data/calder_20261019_07z_work_saturation.png)\n\nThis calculation does not demonstrate that the physical interbraid constraint is inverse-cubic.\n\nIt demonstrates that **if the historical inverse-cubic expression is used with fixed coefficient and radial separation, it cannot establish confinement through divergent work**.\n\n---\n\n# 5. The original interaction potential\n\nFor three filaments with phase offsets:\n\n\\[\n\\delta_1,\\delta_2,\\delta_3,\n\\]\n\nthe historical interaction potential is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_{\\mathrm{int}}\n=\nkR^2\n\\sum_{i<j}\n\\left[\n1-\\cos(\\delta_i-\\delta_j)\n\\right].\n}\n\\]\n\nHere \\(R\\) is the common radius and \\(k\\) is the interaction coefficient.\n\nThe symmetric configuration is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\boldsymbol\\delta_0=\n\\left(\n0,\\frac{2\\pi}{3},\\frac{4\\pi}{3}\n\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nIts gradient vanishes:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\nabla_\\delta V(\\boldsymbol\\delta_0)=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe phase Hessian is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nH_{\\mathrm{phase}}\n=\nkR^2\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n-1&1/2&1/2\\\\\n1/2&-1&1/2\\\\\n1/2&1/2&-1\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\]\n\nIts eigenvalues are:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\lambda=\n\\left\\{\n0,\n-\\frac32kR^2,\n-\\frac32kR^2\n\\right\\}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor \\(k>0\\), the two relative-phase modes have negative curvature.\n\nThe zero eigenvalue corresponds to uniform phase rotation.\n\nThese are the original, recoverable results.\n\n---\n\n# 4. The ambient four-dimensional construction\n\nNow consider three vectors in four-dimensional Euclidean space:\n\n\\[\nX_i\\in\\mathbb R^4.\n\\]\n\nDefine:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nF(X_1,X_2,X_3)\n=\n\\frac{k}{2}\n\\sum_{i<j}\n|X_i-X_j|^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is the ambient quadratic pair-distance interaction used in the historical audit.\n\nIts Hessian is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nH_{\\mathrm{ambient}}\n=\nkC\\otimes I_4,\n}\n\\]\n\nwhere:\n\n\\[\nC=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n2&-1&-1\\\\\n-1&2&-1\\\\\n-1&-1&2\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nThe eigenvalues of \\(C\\) are:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\{0,3,3\\}.}\n\\]\n\nTherefore the ambient twelve-dimensional Hessian has:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\lambda_{\\mathrm{ambient}}\n=\n\\{0^{\\times4},(3k)^{\\times8}\\}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor \\(k>0\\), this is positive semidefinite.\n\nThat result is correct.\n\nBut it is not yet the Hessian of the fixed-radius phase system.\n\n---\n\n# 5. The missing geometric term\n\nDefine the fixed-radius embedding:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nX_i(\\delta_i)=\nR\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n\\cos\\delta_i\\\\\n\\sin\\delta_i\\\\\n0\\\\\n0\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\]\n\nSubstitution into the ambient interaction \\(X(\\delta)\\), the Hessian of the restricted function is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nH_{\\mathrm{phase}}\n=\nJ^TH_{\\mathrm{ambient}}J\n+\n\\sum_a\n\\frac{\\partial F}{\\partial X_a}\n\\frac{\\partial^2X_a}\n{\\partial\\delta_i\\partial\\delta_j}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe first term is the ordinary pullback of the ambient Hessian.\n\nThe second term accounts for the curvature of the Euclidean tube: Exact derivation\n\nUse four-dimensional coordinates:\n\n\\[\n(w,x,y,z).\n\\]\n\nAll four coordinates have dimensions of length.\n\nLet the centerline be:\n\n\\[\nL(t)=(t,\\beta t,0,0).\n\\]\n\nThe squared Euclidean distance from an arbitrary point to a point on the centerline is:\n\n\\[\nD^2(t)\n=\n(w-t)^2+(x-\\beta t)^2+y^2+z^2.\n\\]\n\nMinimize over \\(t\\).\n\nDifferentiation gives:\n\n\\[\n\\frac{dD^2}{dt}\n=\n-2(w-t)-2\\beta(x-\\beta t).\n\\]\n\nSetting the derivative to zero:\n\n\\[\nt_*=\n\\frac{w+\\beta x}{1+\\beta^2}.\n\\]\n\nSubstituting:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_E^2\n=\n\\frac{(x-\\beta w)^2}{1+\\beta^2}\n+y^2+z^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nA solid Euclidean tube of radius \\(a\\) satisfies:\n\n\\[\nd_E^2\\leq a^2.\n\\]\n\nAt the instantaneous slice:\n\n\\[\nw=0,\n\\]\n\nthe intersection becomes:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{x^2}{a^2(1+\\beta^2)}\n+\n\\frac{y^2}{a^2}\n+\n\\frac{z^2}{a^2}\n\\leq1.\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore its semiaxes are:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\left(\na\\sqrt{1+\\beta^2},a,a\n\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\n**Symbolic derivation: PASS.**\n\n---\n\n# 4. Test A: Gauss linking symmetry\n\nFor two disjoint, oriented closed curves in three-dimensional Euclidean space, the Gauss linking integral is:\n\n\\[\nLk(C_1,C_2)\n=\n\\frac1{4\\pi}\n\\oint_{C_1}\\oint_{C_2}\n\\frac{\n(\\mathbf r_1-\\mathbf r_2)\n\\cdot\n(d\\mathbf r_1\\times d\\mathbf r_2)\n}{\n|\\mathbf r_1-\\mathbf r_2|^3\n}.\n\\]\n\nExchange the two curve labels.\n\nThe displacement reverses:\n\n\\[\n\\mathbf r_2-\\mathbf r_1\n=\n-(\\mathbf r_1-\\mathbf r_2).\n\\]\n\nThe cross product also reverses:\n\n\\[\nd\\mathbf r_2\\times d\\mathbf r_1\n=\n-(d\\mathbf r_1\\times d\\mathbf r_2).\n\\]\n\nConsequently:\n\n\\[\n(-\\mathbf r)\\cdot(-\\mathbf a)\n=\n\\mathbf r\\cdot\\mathbf a.\n\\]\n\nThe integrand retains its sign.\n\nTherefore:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nLk(C_1,C_2)=Lk(C_2,C_1).\n}\n\\]\n\n**The ordinary Gauss linking number is symmetric under exchanging the two oriented components.**\n\nReversing the orientation of just one component changes the sign. Exchanging their labels does not.\n\n### Numerical verification\n\nTwo explicit circles were constructed:\n\n\\[\nC_1(t)=\n(\\cos t,\\sin t,0)\n\\]\n\nand:\n\n\\[\nC_2(s)=\n(0,1+\\cos s,\\sin s).\n\\]\n\nThe double integral was evaluated using independent periodic discretizations.\n\n| Grid resolution | \\(Lk(C_1,C_2)\\) | \\(Lk(C_2,C_1)\\) |\n|---|---:|---:|\n| 80 × 80 | −1.000000000000 | −1.000000000000 |\n| 160 × 160 | −1.000000000000 | −1.000000000000 |\n| 320 × 320 | −1.000000000000 | −1.000000000000 |\n\nA translated, unlinked control returned zero.\n\nThree continuous offsets preserving the linked configuration also returned −1.\n\nThe corresponding finite-difference derivative was zero at the printed precision.\n\n**Result: The historical antisymmetry claim FAILS.**\n\n---\n\n# 4. The geometrical question\n\nConsider four-dimensional coordinates:\n\n\\[\nX=(w,x,y,z)\n\\]\n\nwith:\n\n\\[\nw=ct.\n\\]\n\nTime is measured in length units.\n\nChoose a straight centerline:\n\n\\[\nx=\\beta w\n\\]\n\nwhere:\n\n\\[\n\\beta=\\frac vc,\n\\qquad 0\\leq\\beta<1.\n\\]\n\nThe resolving time surface is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{w=0.}\n\\]\n\nLet:\n\n\\[\na>0\n\\]\n\nbe the intrinsic normal-fiber radius and:\n\n\\[\nL>0\n\\]\n\nthe finite axial support length.\n\nThese are mathematical fixture parameters, not empirically established particle dimensions.\n\nThe question is:\n\n**How does the intersection change when normal distance is defined using Euclidean geometry rather than Minkowski geometry?**\n\n---\n\n# 4. Euclidean normal-fiber construction\n\nBegin with:\n\n\\[\n\\delta=\n\\operatorname{diag}(1,1,1,1).\n\\]\n\nThe normalized centerline direction is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nu_E=\n\\frac{(1,\\beta,0,0)}\n{\\sqrt{1+\\beta^2}}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor a point \\(X\\), define its squared normal distance:\n\n\\[\nr_E^2=\n\\delta(X,X)-\\delta(X,u_E)^2.\n\\]\n\nOn the time surface:\n\n\\[\nX=(0,x,y,z).\n\\]\n\nSubstitution gives:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nr_E^2=\n\\frac{x^2}{1+\\beta^2}+y^2+z^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe finite-core condition is:\n\n\\[\nr_E^2\\leq a^2.\n\\]\n\nTherefore:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{x^2}{a^2(1+\\beta^2)}\n+\n\\frac{y^2}{a^2}\n+\n\\frac{z^2}{a^2}\n\\leq1.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor an infinitely extended straight tube, the intersection is an ellipsoid with semiaxes:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\na\\sqrt{1+\\beta^2},\\quad a,\\quad a.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe intersection elongates as \\(\\beta\\) increases.\n\n## The angle-convention issue\n\nBEDROCK BR-005 defines \\(\\theta_4\\) from the time normal.\n\nFor this straight Euclidean-coordinate fixture:\n\n\\[\n\\theta_4=\\arctan\\beta.\n\\]\n\nConsequently:\n\n\\[\n\\cos\\theta_4=\n\\frac1{\\sqrt{1+\\beta^2}}.\n\\]\n\nThe long semiaxis becomes:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\na_{\\parallel}=\\frac a{\\cos\\theta_4}.\n}\n\\]\n\nBut ND-2026-10-18-07 records the oblique-slice formula:\n\n\\[\na_{\\parallel}=\\frac a{|\\sin\\theta|}.\n\\]\n\nThese expressions are not necessarily contradictory.\n\nIf \\(\\theta\\) is measured from the sheet rather than its normal, then:\n\n\\[\n\\theta=\\frac\\pi2-\\theta_4.\n\\]\n\nThus:\n\n\\[\n\\sin\\theta=\\cos\\theta_4\n\\]\n\nand:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac a{\\sin\\theta}\n=\n\\frac a{\\cos\\theta_4}.\n}\n\\]\n\n**The formulas agree exactly under complementary angle conventions.**\n\nWhat fails is identifying the two differently defined angles without performing the conversion.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Minkowski Fermi-normal construction\n\nNow use:\n\n\\[\n\\eta=\n\\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1).\n\\]\n\nThe normalized timelike centerline tangent is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nu_M=\n\\frac{(1,\\beta,0,0)}\n{\\sqrt{1-\\beta^2}}.\n}\n\\]\n\nIt satisfies:\n\n\\[\n\\eta(u_M,u_M)=-1.\n\\]\n\nDefine the squared spacelike distance orthogonal to this timelike direction:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nr_M^2=\n\\eta(X,X)+\\eta(X,u_M)^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nOn:\n\n\\[\nw=0,\n\\]\n\nthe expression becomes:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nr_M^2=\n\\frac{x^2}{1-\\beta^2}+y^2+z^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe finite-core condition is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{x^2}{a^2(1-\\beta^2)}\n+\n\\frac{y^2}{a^2}\n+\n\\frac{z^2}{a^2}\n\\leq1.\n}\n\\]\n\nIts semiaxes are:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\na\\sqrt{1-\\beta^2},\\quad a,\\quad a.\n}\n\\]\n\nWriting:\n\n\\[\n\\gamma=\\frac1{\\sqrt{1-\\beta^2}},\n\\]\n\nthe axial semiaxis is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\na_{\\parallel}=\\frac a\\gamma.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis construction contracts its time-surface intersection along the direction of motion.\n\nThat is the opposite dependence from the Euclidean construction.\n\nThe result follows from the metric used to define the normal fiber. It does not independently establish which construction represents a physical SAT/H(s)H core.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Finite axial support\n\nThe preceding ellipsoids assume infinite centerline support.\n\nNow impose:\n\n\\[\n|\\lambda|\\leq\\frac L2.\n\\]\n\nFor the Euclidean construction:\n\n\\[\n\\lambda_E=\n\\frac{\\beta x}{\\sqrt{1+\\beta^2}}.\n\\]\n\nFor the Minkowski construction:\n\n\\[\n|\\lambda_M|=\n\\frac{\\beta|x|}{\\sqrt{1-\\beta^2}}.\n\\]\n\nDefine:\n\n\\[\nk_E=\\sqrt{1+\\beta^2}\n\\]\n\nand:\n\n\\[\nk_M=\\sqrt{1-\\beta^2}.\n\\]\n\nThe slice condition in either case becomes:\n\n\\[\n\\frac{x^2}{k^2}+y^2+z^2\\leq a^2\n\\]\n\nwith:\n\n\\[\n|x|\\leq\n\\frac{kL}{2\\beta}.\n\\]\n\nDefine:\n\n\\[\nq_{\\max}=\n\\min\\left(a,\\frac L{2\\beta}\\right)\n\\]\n\nfor \\(\\beta>0\\), and \\(q_{\\max}=a\\) at rest.\n\nThen:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|x|\\leq kq_{\\max}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe finite tube's slice is an ellipsoid, possibly truncated by its axial ends.\n\n---\n\n# 7. The resulting formulas are not claimed to apply unchanged to finite, helical, or hollow worldtubes.\n\n---\n\n# 3. Minkowski construction\n\nUse four-dimensional coordinates:\n\n\\[\nX=(w,x,y,z)\n\\]\n\nwith:\n\n\\[\nw=ct.\n\\]\n\nAll four coordinates have dimensions of length.\n\nThe metric is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\eta=\\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1).\n}\n\\]\n\nConsider a straight centerline:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nx=\\beta w\n}\n\\]\n\nwhere:\n\n\\[\n\\beta=\\frac vc,\\qquad 0\\leq\\beta<1.\n\\]\n\nIts normalized timelike tangent is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nu=\n\\frac{(1,\\beta,0,0)}\n{\\sqrt{1-\\beta^2}}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe squared spacelike distance from the centerline is:\n\n\\[\nr_\\perp^2=\n\\eta(X,X)+\\eta(X,u)^2.\n\\]\n\nSymbolic simplification gives:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nr_\\perp^2=\n\\frac{(x-\\beta w)^2}{1-\\beta^2}\n+y^2+z^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor a worldtube of proper normal radius \\(a\\):\n\n\\[\nr_\\perp^2\\leq a^2.\n\\]\n\nDefine:\n\n\\[\nk=\\sqrt{1-\\beta^2}.\n\\]\n\nAt any fixed value of \\(w\\), the intersection is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{(x-\\beta w)^2}{k^2}\n+y^2+z^2\\leq a^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is an ellipsoid centered at:\n\n\\[\nx=\\beta w.\n\\]\n\nIts semiaxes are:\n\n\\[\nka,\\quad a,\\quad a.\n\\]\n\nTherefore its volume is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_0=\\frac{4\\pi}{3}ka^3.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is the instantaneous slice volume.\n\n**Symbolic derivation: PASS.**\n\n---\n\n# 4. Introduce a finite resolving slab\n\nLet the resolving time interval be:\n\n\\[\n-\\frac{\\Delta}{2}\n\\leq w\\leq\n\\frac{\\Delta}{2}.\n\\]\n\nHere:\n\n\\[\n\\Delta=c\\Delta t.\n\\]\n\nThe resolving thickness \\(\\Delta\\) has dimensions of length.\n\nThe question is what three-dimensional structure the resolving process returns.\n\nThere are at least two mathematically distinct possibilities.\n\n## A. Union of occupied regions\n\nDefine:\n\n\\[\nU_\\Delta=\n\\bigcup_{|w|\\leq\\Delta/2}E_w\n\\]\n\nwhere \\(E_w\\) is the ellipsoidal slice at \\(w\\).\n\nThis operator includes every spatial point occupied at any time during the interval.\n\nBecause the ellipsoid translates along the \\(x\\)-axis, the union is the Minkowski sum of the original ellipsoid and a line segment of length:\n\n\\[\n\\beta\\Delta.\n\\]\n\nThe union volume is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_{\\mathrm{union}}\n=\n\\frac{4\\pi}{3}ka^3\n+\n\\pi a^2\\beta\\Delta.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe first term is the instantaneous ellipsoid volume.\n\nThe second is the volume swept out by its transverse projection.\n\nThe ratio is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{V_{\\mathrm{union}}}{V_0}\n=\n1+\\frac{3\\beta\\Delta}{4ka}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis quantity increases with resolving thickness.\n\nBut it is not an instantaneous particle volume.\n\nIt includes points occupied at different times.\n\n---\n\n## B. Time-averaged occupancy\n\nNow define:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nO_\\Delta(x,y,z)\n=\n\\frac1\\Delta\n\\int_{-\\Delta/2}^{\\Delta/2}\n\\mathbf1_{E_w}(x,y,z)\\,dw.\n}\n\\]\n\nHere \\(\\mathbf1_{E_w}\\) is the indicator function of the ellipsoid.\n\nThe result is a fractional occupancy field.\n\nA point occupied throughout the resolving interval has:\n\n\\[\nO_\\Delta=1.\n\\]\n\nA point occupied during half the interval has:\n\n\\[\nO_\\Delta=\\frac12.\n\\]\n\nA point never occupied has:\n\n\\[\nO_\\Delta=0.\n\\]\n\nIntegrate this field over three-dimensional space:\n\n\\[\n\\int_{\\mathbb R^3}\nO_\\Delta\\,d^3x.\n\\]\n\nExchange the spatial and temporal integrals:\n\n\\[\n=\n\\frac1\\Delta\n\\int_{-\\Delta/2}^{\\Delta/2}\n\\left(\n\\int_{\\mathbb R^3}\n\\mathbf1_{E_w}\\,d^3x\n\\right)dw.\n\\]\n\nEvery instantaneous ellipsoid has volume \\(V_0\\).\n\nTherefore:\n\n\\[\n=\n\\frac1\\Delta\n\\int_{-\\Delta/2}^{\\Delta/2}\nV_0\\,dw.\n\\]\n\nHence:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\int_{\\mathbb R^3}\nO_\\Delta\\,d^3x=V_0.\n}\n\\]\n\n**The integrated time-averaged occupancy does not increase with resolving thickness.**\n\nThat differs from the union volume.\n\nThe distinction follows directly from the definitions.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Exact occupancy function\n\nAt transverse radius:\n\n\\[\n\\rho=\\sqrt{y^2+z^2}\n\\]\n\ndefine:\n\n\\[\nq=k\\sqrt{a^2-\\rho^2}.\n\\]\n\nFor \\(\\rho<a\\), the point lies inside the instantaneous ellipsoid when:\n\n\\[\n|x-\\beta w|\\leq q.\n\\]\n\nFor \\(\\beta>0\\), solve for the permitted interval in \\(w\\):\n\n\\[\n\\frac{x-q}{\\beta}\n\\leq w\\leq\n\\frac{x+q}{\\beta}.\n\\]\n\nIntersect that interval with the resolving slab.\n\nThe exact occupancy is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nO_\\Delta=\n\\frac1\\Delta\n\\max\\left[\n0,\\,\n\\min\\left(\\frac\\Delta2,\\frac{x+q}{\\beta}\\right)\n-\n\\max\\left(-\\frac\\Delta2,\\frac{x-q}{\\beta}\\right)\n\\right].\n}\n\\]\n\nFor \\(\\beta=0\\), the expression is replaced by the stationary ellipsoid indicator.\n\nThis function was evaluated numerically and integrated independently.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Second-moment calculation\n\nThere is another way to characterize the apparent intersection.\n\nInstead of measuring the union volume, consider the spatial variance of the time-averaged occupancy distribution.\n\nWrite:\n\n\\[\nx=x_0+\\beta w.\n\\]\n\nHere \\(x_0\\) is uniformly distributed inside the stationary ellipsoid and \\(w\\) uniformly distributed over the resolving slab.\n\nFor the ellipsoid:\n\n\\[\n\\operatorname{Var}(x_0)=\\frac{k^2a^2}{5}.\n\\]\n\nFor the uniform resolving interval:\n\n\\[\n\\operatorname{Var}(w)=\\frac{\\Delta^2}{12}.\n\\]\n\nBecause the variables are independent:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{Var}(x)\n=\n\\frac{k^2a^2}{5}\n+\n\\frac{\\beta^2\\Delta^2}{12}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe transverse variances remain:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{Var}(y)\n=\n\\operatorname{Var}(z)\n=\n\\frac{a^2}{5}.\n}\n\\]\n\nA second-moment-equivalent ellipsoid would therefore have an effective axial semiaxis:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\na_{\\mathrm{eff}}\n=\n\\sqrt{\nk^2a^2+\\frac5{12}\\beta^2\\Delta^2\n}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis differs from the axial half-extent of the union:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\na_{\\mathrm{union}}\n=\nka+\\frac{\\beta\\Delta}{2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThus the same worldtube and resolving slab produce different apparent dimensions depending on the chosen measurement functional.\n\n---\n\n# 7. The bounded mathematical question\n\nThe preceding Mercer calculation established that an infinitely extended straight Minkowski worldtube has a constant instantaneous slice volume.\n\nConsequently, averaging those slices across a finite resolving interval leaves their integrated occupancy unchanged.\n\nBut the earlier Ravel construction makes finite axial support available as an explicit geometric constraint.\n\nThe question is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{Does slab-volume invariance survive finite axial support?}\n}\n\\]\n\nThe answer is no, in general.\n\nThe calculation below uses a finite **proper-duration** worldtube as a precisely defined mathematical fixture.\n\nThis does not assume that physical particles have a finite lifetime equal to the fixture parameter \\(L\\).\n\n---\n\n# 4. Minkowski construction\n\nUse:\n\n\\[\nX=(w,x,y,z)\n\\]\n\nwith:\n\n\\[\nw=ct.\n\\]\n\nThe metric is:\n\n\\[\n\\eta=\n\\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1).\n\\]\n\nDefine:\n\n\\[\n\\beta=\\frac vc,\n\\qquad\nk=\\sqrt{1-\\beta^2}.\n\\]\n\nThe timelike centerline is:\n\n\\[\nx=\\beta w.\n\\]\n\nIntroduce the proper axial coordinate \\(\\tau\\) and spacelike normal coordinate \\(q\\).\n\nThe Lorentz transformation is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nw=\\frac{\\tau+\\beta q}{k}\n}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nx=\\frac{q+\\beta\\tau}{k}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe inverse transformation gives:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nq=\\frac{x-\\beta w}{k}\n}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\tau=\\frac{w-\\beta x}{k}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe finite worldtube is defined by:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n-\\frac L2\\leq\\tau\\leq\\frac L2\n}\n\\]\n\nand:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nq^2+y^2+z^2\\leq a^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nHere \\(a\\) is the proper normal radius and \\(L\\) is the finite proper axial extent.\n\nBoth have dimensions of length.\n\n### Jacobian check\n\nThe transformation matrix is:\n\n\\[\n\\frac1k\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n1&\\beta\\\\\n\\beta&1\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nIts determinant is:\n\n\\[\n\\frac{1-\\beta^2}{k^2}=1.\n\\]\n\nTherefore:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ndw\\,dx= d\\tau\\,dq\n}\n\\]\n\nwhen interpreted with the corresponding orientation.\n\n**Symbolic test: PASS.**\n\n---\n\n# 5. Exact instantaneous intersection volume\n\nAt fixed \\(w\\), the inverse transformation gives:\n\n\\[\n\\tau=kw-\\beta q.\n\\]\n\nThe finite axial-support condition becomes:\n\n\\[\n\\left|kw-\\beta q\\right|\n\\leq\\frac L2.\n\\]\n\nFor \\(\\beta>0\\), the permitted interval is:\n\n\\[\nq_-\n=\n\\max\\left(\n-a,\\frac{kw-L/2}{\\beta}\n\\right)\n\\]\n\nand:\n\n\\[\nq_+\n=\n\\min\\left(\na,\\frac{kw+L/2}{\\beta}\n\\right).\n\\]\n\nAt each \\(q\\), the transverse disk has area:\n\n\\[\nA(q)=\\pi(a^2-q^2).\n\\]\n\nBecause:\n\n\\[\ndx=k\\,dq\n\\]\n\non a fixed-\\(w\\) slice, the three-dimensional volume is:\n\n\\[\nV(w)=\n\\pi k\n\\int_{q_-}^{q_+}\n(a^2-q^2)\\,dq.\n\\]\n\nIntegrating:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV(w)=\n\\pi k\n\\left[\na^2(q_+-q_-)\n-\n\\frac{q_+^3-q_-^3}{3}\n\\right]\n}\n\\]\n\nwhen \\(q_+>q_-\\).\n\nOtherwise:\n\n\\[\nV(w)=0.\n\\]\n\nUnlike the infinite-duration construction, this volume depends on the resolving time coordinate.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Exact finite-slab average\n\nDefine the resolving slab:\n\n\\[\n-\\frac{\\Delta}{2}\n\\leq w\\leq\n\\frac{\\Delta}{2}.\n\\]\n\nThe spatially integrated time-averaged occupancy is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\overline V(\\Delta)\n=\n\\frac1\\Delta\n\\int_{-\\Delta/2}^{\\Delta/2}\nV(w)\\,dw.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe integral can be evaluated analytically.\n\nFor \\(\\beta>0\\), define:\n\n\\[\nQ_1=\n\\frac{k\\Delta+L}{2\\beta}\n\\]\n\nand:\n\n\\[\nQ_0=\n\\frac{|k\\Delta-L|}{2\\beta}.\n\\]\n\nFor positive \\(Q\\), let:\n\n\\[\nm=\\min(a,Q).\n\\]\n\nDefine:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nJ(Q)=\n2\\left[\na^2Qm\n-\\frac{a^2m^2}{2}\n-\\frac{Qm^3}{3}\n+\\frac{m^4}{4}\n\\right].\n}\n\\]\n\nFor \\(Q\\leq0\\), set \\(J(Q)=0\\).\n\nThen:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\overline V(\\Delta)\n=\n\\frac{\\pi\\beta}{\\Delta}\n\\left[\nJ(Q_1)-J(Q_0)\n\\right].\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is the exact finite-duration, finite-slab result for the declared straight-tube fixture.\n\nIt requires no fitted coefficients.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Exact global intersection calculation\n\nConsider two distinct points on the circular worldline.\n\nBy rotational symmetry, choose their orbital angles as:\n\n\\[\n-\\alpha,\\qquad+\\alpha.\n\\]\n\nTheir spacetime positions are:\n\n\\[\nX_-=\n\\left(\n-\\frac{R\\alpha}{\\beta},\nR\\cos\\alpha,\n-R\\sin\\alpha,\n0\n\\right)\n\\]\n\nand:\n\n\\[\nX_+=\n\\left(\n\\frac{R\\alpha}{\\beta},\nR\\cos\\alpha,\nR\\sin\\alpha,\n0\n\\right).\n\\]\n\nA spacetime point \\(P=(w,x,y,z)\\) belongs to the normal hyperplane at \\(X_-\\) when:\n\n\\[\nU_-\\cdot(P-X_-)=0.\n\\]\n\nSimilarly:\n\n\\[\nU_+\\cdot(P-X_+)=0.\n\\]\n\nExpanding these conditions gives:\n\n\\[\nw+\\frac{R\\alpha}{\\beta}\n=\n\\beta(\\sin\\alpha\\,x+\\cos\\alpha\\,y)\n\\]\n\nand:\n\n\\[\nw-\\frac{R\\alpha}{\\beta}\n=\n\\beta(-\\sin\\alpha\\,x+\\cos\\alpha\\,y).\n\\]\n\nSolving simultaneously:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nx=\n\\frac{R\\alpha}{\\beta^2\\sin\\alpha}\n}\n\\]\n\nand:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nw=\\beta\\cos\\alpha\\,y.\n}\n\\]\n\nWhen \\(\\alpha=n\\pi\\neq0\\), these equations have no finite common solution.\n\nFor all other nonzero \\(\\alpha\\), the two normal hyperplanes intersect in a two-dimensional plane.\n\nThe remaining question is whether their finite-radius normal balls overlap.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Minimize the required common radius\n\nFor any point in the common normal-hyperplane intersection, calculate the squared Minkowski normal distance to each footpoint.\n\nThe two results can be written:\n\n\\[\nr_-^2=\nr_0^2+Cy^2+2Dy+z^2\n\\]\n\nand:\n\n\\[\nr_+^2=\nr_0^2+Cy^2-2Dy+z^2\n\\]\n\nwhere:\n\n\\[\nC=1-\\beta^2\\cos^2\\alpha>0\n\\]\n\nand:\n\n\\[\nD=R(\\sin\\alpha-\\alpha\\cos\\alpha).\n\\]\n\nTo find the smallest radius at which both normal balls could contain the same point, minimize:\n\n\\[\n\\max(r_-^2,r_+^2).\n\\]\n\nSince:\n\n\\[\n\\max(r_-^2,r_+^2)\n=\nr_0^2+Cy^2+2|Dy|+z^2,\n\\]\n\nthe minimum occurs at:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ny=z=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe corresponding squared common radius is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nr_0^2=\nR^2\n\\left[\n\\frac{\\alpha^2}{\\beta^4\\sin^2\\alpha}\n-\\frac{2\\alpha\\cot\\alpha}{\\beta^2}\n+1-\\frac{\\alpha^2}{\\beta^2}\n\\right].\n}\n\\]\n\nThis expression determines the global contact radius for any chosen pair of footpoints.\n\nNow compare it with the local focal radius:\n\n\\[\nr_f=\n\\frac{R(1-\\beta^2)}{\\beta^2}.\n\\]\n\nSubtracting and factoring gives the central identity:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nr_0^2-r_f^2=\n\\frac{R^2}{\\beta^4}\n\\left[\n(1-\\beta^2)\n\\left(\n\\frac{\\alpha^2}{\\sin^2\\alpha}-1\n\\right)\n+\n\\beta^2\n(\\alpha\\cot\\alpha-1)^2\n\\right].\n}\n\\]\n\nBoth terms inside the brackets are nonnegative.\n\nFor the first:\n\n\\[\n|\\sin\\alpha|\\leq|\\alpha|\n\\]\n\nimplies:\n\n\\[\n\\frac{\\alpha^2}{\\sin^2\\alpha}-1\\geq0.\n\\]\n\nThe second term is a square.\n\nTherefore:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nr_0^2\\geq r_f^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor distinct footpoints with finite intersection, the inequality is strict.\n\nAs:\n\n\\[\n\\alpha\\rightarrow0,\n\\]\n\nthe common radius approaches the local focal radius:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nr_0\\rightarrow r_f.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis establishes the exact result.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Theorem: Global and local thresholds coincide\n\nFor the specified circular timelike worldline in flat Minkowski spacetime, equipped with uniform round Fermi normal balls:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\na<\n\\frac{R(1-\\beta^2)}{\\beta^2}\n}\n\\]\n\nis sufficient for global injectivity.\n\nIt is also sharp.\n\nAt equality, the local Fermi Jacobian becomes singular.\n\nFor any larger radius, sufficiently nearby but distinct normal fibers intersect.\n\nConsequently:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{Global reach}\n=\n\\text{Local focal radius}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis result holds for the stated circular fixture.\n\nIt does not establish the same property for arbitrary accelerated worldlines, finite helices, nonround cores, or interacting worldtube networks.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Exact geometrical calculation\n\nLet the underlying construction space be:\n\n\\[\n\\mathbb R^4\n\\]\n\nwith Euclidean metric:\n\n\\[\n\\delta=I_4.\n\\]\n\nLet \\(u\\) be a unit flow director:\n\n\\[\nu^Tu=1.\n\\]\n\nDefine the orthogonal timesheet projector:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{P=I-uu^T}\n\\]\n\nand the Householder operator:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{H=I-2uu^T}.\n\\]\n\nEvery vector can be decomposed as:\n\n\\[\nv=au+w\n\\]\n\nwhere:\n\n\\[\nu^Tw=0.\n\\]\n\nThen:\n\n\\[\nPv=w\n\\]\n\nand:\n\n\\[\nHv=-au+w.\n\\]\n\nThis immediately determines both operators' eigenvalues.\n\n### Timesheet projector\n\nFor \\(P\\):\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\operatorname{spec}(P)=\\{0,1,1,1\\}}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\operatorname{rank}(P)=3}\n\\]\n\nand:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\det P=0}.\n\\]\n\nRestricted to the three-dimensional subspace perpendicular to \\(u\\), the projector acts as the identity.\n\nIts intrinsic three-volume Jacobian is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{J_3=1}.\n\\]\n\n### Householder operator\n\nFor \\(H\\):\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\operatorname{spec}(H)=\\{-1,1,1,1\\}}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\det H=-1}.\n\\]\n\nIts absolute determinant is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{|\\det H|=1}.\n\\]\n\nFurthermore:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{H^2=I}.\n\\]\n\nThe operator reverses one direction while preserving lengths and absolute four-volume.\n\nNeither determinant produces:\n\n\\[\nB^4.\n\\]\n\n---\n\n# 4. A stronger test: Oblique three-dimensional projection\n\nPerhaps the four powers arise because the timesheet is tilted relative to the filament's natural frame.\n\nWe can test that explicitly.\n\nConsider two three-dimensional hyperplanes in four-dimensional Euclidean space.\n\nLet their unit normals differ by angle \\(\\theta\\).\n\nChoose coordinates such that the source normal is:\n\n\\[\nu=(0,0,0,1)\n\\]\n\nand the target normal is:\n\n\\[\nn=(\\sin\\theta,0,0,\\cos\\theta).\n\\]\n\nThe target projector is:\n\n\\[\nP_n=I-nn^T.\n\\]\n\nRestrict this map to the source three-plane.\n\nThe Gram matrix of the projected source basis is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n\\cos^2\\theta&0&0\\\\\n0&1&0\\\\\n0&0&1\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\]\n\nIts determinant is:\n\n\\[\n\\det G=\\cos^2\\theta.\n\\]\n\nThe three-dimensional volume Jacobian is therefore:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nJ_3=\\sqrt{\\det G}=|\\cos\\theta|.\n}\n\\]\n\n**A single oblique three-plane projection produces one cosine factor, not four.**\n\nIf we identify:\n\n\\[\nB=|\\cos\\theta|,\n\\]\n\nthen:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{J_3=B}.\n\\]\n\nIt does not follow that:\n\n\\[\nJ_3=B^4.\n\\]\n\nTo obtain \\(B^4\\) as a Jacobian, one possible mathematical construction is:\n\n\\[\nD=BI_4.\n\\]\n\nThis gives:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\det D=B^4}.\n\\]\n\nBut \\(D\\) is an additional uniform contraction of four dimensions.\n\nIt is not the original timesheet projector or the Householder operator.\n\nOther constructions could produce the same factor through repeated interactions, anisotropic deformation, integrated coupling, or a specified physical measure.\n\nThose possibilities remain open.\n\n### Mathematical verdict\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{Bare Householder/timesheet projection}\n\\not\\Rightarrow B^4.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is an exact conditional result.\n\nIt does not establish that the historical electron scaling is physically impossible.\n\nIt establishes that the particular geometrical operators tested here do not, by themselves, derive it.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Independent mass-anchor reconstruction\n\nThe historical laws posit a common mass scale \\(m_0\\).\n\nWe can solve for that scale independently from the electron and proton.\n\nFrom the electron:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nm_{0,e}=\\frac{m_e}{B^4}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFrom the proton:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nm_{0,p}=\\frac{2Bm_p}{3}.\n}\n\\]\n\nIf the declared Holonomy Bridge modifies the proton branch by \\(1+\\Delta\\), then:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nm_{0,p}\n=\n\\frac{2Bm_p}{3(1+\\Delta)}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe two reconstructions must agree if both historical mass laws and the common-anchor assumption hold.\n\nTheir ratio is:\n\n\\[\n\\frac{m_{0,p}}{m_{0,e}}\n=\n\\frac{2B^5m_p}{3(1+\\Delta)m_e}.\n\\]\n\nEquivalently:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{m_{0,p}}{m_{0,e}}\n=\n\\frac{\\mu_{\\mathrm{observed}}}\n{\\mu_{\\mathrm{model}}}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis provides a second way of expressing the mass-ratio consistency test.\n\nIt does not introduce an additional independent empirical datum, because both comparisons ultimately depend on the same proton and electron masses.\n\nHowever, it identifies precisely how the disagreement affects the claimed universal mass anchor.\n\n---\n\n# 6. CODATA comparison\n\nThe benchmark is the entity[\"organization\",\"National Institute of Standards and Technology\",\"United States federal measurement laboratory\"] url2022 CODATA Dimensional reconstruction\n\nThe historical formula is:\n\n\\[\n\\ell_f^3=\\frac{2A}{T}.\n\\]\n\nSince tension has SI dimensions:\n\n\\[\n[T]=\\mathrm N=\\mathrm{J\\,m^{-1}},\n\\]\n\ndimensional homogeneity requires:\n\n\\[\n[A]=[T][\\ell_f]^3.\n\\]\n\nTherefore:\n\n\\[\n[A]=\\mathrm{N\\,m^3}.\n\\]\n\nEquivalently:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{[A]=\\mathrm{J\\,m^2}}.\n\\]\n\nThis is not the ordinary bending-rigidity dimension of an elastic filament.\n\nFor a conventional filament bending-energy functional, the rigidity coefficient \\(K\\) typically has dimensions:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{[K]=\\mathrm{J\\,m}}.\n\\]\n\nConsequently:\n\n\\[\n\\frac KT\n\\]\n\nhas dimensions of length squared.\n\nIts natural length scale is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\ell\\sim\\sqrt{\\frac KT}}.\n\\]\n\nThe historical cube-root formula and the ordinary square-root bending formula are therefore **different geometrical constructions**, not interchangeable notation.\n\nThe separately archived \\(\\kappa\\), measured in joules, is a third dimensional assignment.\n\nIt cannot simply be substituted for either \\(A\\) or \\(K\\).\n\n### Dimensional verdict\n\nThe historical cube-root expression is internally consistent if:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{[A]=\\mathrm{J\\,m^2}}.\n\\]\n\nThe source-defined physical meaning of that coefficient remains unresolved.\n\n---\n\n# 4.
